results.angle_summary: Closest prior art is PUDL: same stack (Parquet + DuckDB + Frictionless Data Package v2 + an agent skill, no MCP). Read its two skills before writing Adele's: they query datapackage.json with jq and never load it whole. No public energy platform that I found does bitemporal as_of over normalized Parquet. Elexon is the only one that exposes publish time as a first-class query axis, so Adele's knowledge-time axis is a real differentiator. Challenges to the spec: (1) borrow oemetadata's timeseries keys (resolutionValue/Unit, alignment, aggregationType) for the adele: block. The spec lacks alignment and aggregation type. (2) Add per-dataset and per-field usage warnings and a license with redistribution limits. Energy-Charts price data for many zones is restricted to internal use. (3) Add a "latest publish time per dataset" endpoint (Elexon) to make freshness cheap. (4) Consider nightly/stable/vDATE path aliases (PUDL) only if reproducibility matters. I found no ready-made self-hosted ENTSO-E pipeline with Parquet and DuckDB.

projects.name: PUDL (Catalyst Cooperative)
projects.what: Open pipeline that fetches, cleans and republishes US energy data (EIA, FERC, EPA) as Parquet files plus a single DuckDB database, with a Frictionless Data Package v2 descriptor.
projects.overlap: Normalization to Parquet, DuckDB as query engine, Frictionless descriptor as catalog, versioned distribution, agent skill.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the docs page: primary format is Parquet at s3://pudl.catalyst.coop/<version>/<table>.parquet, with three path prefixes: nightly/ (rebuilt most weekday mornings, less validated), stable/ (alias to the latest release) and vYYYY.M.P/ (immutable; also archived on Zenodo with a DOI). One pudl_parquet_datapackage.json lists column types, constraints and foreign keys for every table; a pudl.duckdb (about 9 GB) is published next to it; SQLite is deprecated and will stop in 2027. A separate descriptor for the large FERC EQR set carries the size and SHA-256 of every file (useful idea for Adele's incremental pull: a manifest with hashes per partition). A web viewer (data.catalyst.coop) shows table metadata and previews. Ideas for Adele: path aliases latest/ and dated snapshots; hash and size per partition in the descriptor; one package-level descriptor in addition to one per dataset. Not reusable as a whole: US data, batch releases, no knowledge-time axis, no per-user keys.
projects.status: Code MIT, data CC-BY-4.0. Active: latest release v2026.11.0 on 10 Nov 2026, monthly releases before that (seen on the GitHub releases page). Orchestrator not verified.

projects.name: Catalyst Cooperative agent-skills (pudl + datapackage skills)
projects.what: Two agent skills: a generic 'datapackage' skill that teaches an agent to explore any Frictionless descriptor, and a 'pudl' skill built on top of it for PUDL data.
projects.overlap: The Skill part of the spec (SKILL.md, progressive disclosure, no MCP) and the choice of Frictionless descriptors as the contract read by the agent.
projects.takeaways: Verified from the two SKILL.md files. datapackage skill (about 1,100 words): rule 'never load the full datapackage.json into context', query it selectively with jq (patterns in a separate reference file metadata-querying.md), surface usage warnings before presenting a resource, check primary and foreign keys before joins, ask the user before loading data, handles descriptor v1 and v2. pudl skill: requires the datapackage skill; a script fetch_descriptor.py caches the descriptor locally and reuses it when it is less than one day old (--force to bypass); for 'does the catalog have X' questions the agent must run a keyword search over metadata and flag any answer that came from memory; down-select at the reader (DuckDB LIMIT, polars scan_parquet); reference files for data access, data quality (table tiers and warning types), methodology, and 'datapackage extensions' (PUDL-specific descriptor fields such as provenance and a unit registry; I could not open that file, 404 on the guessed path). Layout: skills/pudl/{SKILL.md, references/, scripts/, assets/}. Installed with 'npx skills add catalyst-cooperative/agent-skills -s pudl'. For Adele: the generic datapackage skill may be usable as is under the Adele skill, and 'adele describe' plays the role of the jq queries. Copy the rules on warnings, on answers from memory and on the descriptor cache.
projects.status: MIT (repo), skill text CC-BY-4.0. Described as experimental. 148 commits, 3 stars; pudl SKILL.md metadata says last updated 2026-08-15. Date of last commit not verified.

projects.name: oemetadata (Open Energy Platform metadata standard)
projects.what: JSON metadata standard for energy datasets, based on Frictionless Data Package and FAIR, used by the Open Energy Platform.
projects.overlap: The catalog descriptor and the 'adele:' extension block (resolution, units per field, time semantics).
projects.takeaways: Verified in metadata_key_description.md (version OEMetadata-2.0). Temporal block: referenceDate, and timeseries[] with start, end, resolutionValue, resolutionUnit, alignment, aggregationType. Per field: name, description, type, nullable, unit, isAbout[] (ontology links), valueReference[] (meaning of coded values). Also sources[] with sourceLicenses, licenses[] with attribution and instruction, primaryKey, foreignKeys, dialect, and a review badge (Iron to Platinum). For Adele: take alignment (does the timestamp mark the start or the end of the interval) and aggregationType (average, sum, instantaneous) into the adele: block, and valueReference for code lists such as bidding zones or PSR types. The spec fixes half-open intervals globally but aggregation type differs per field (MW average versus MWh sum). oemetadata has no fields for freshness, next refresh, revision policy or knowledge time: those stay Adele-specific. Adopting the full standard would be too heavy (ontology links, review process).
projects.status: Code MIT, schema CC0. Release date not shown on the page (not checked).

projects.name: Elexon Insights Solution API (BMRS)
projects.what: Public API of the GB balancing and settlement data, replacing the legacy BMRS.
projects.overlap: Knowledge time versus delivery time, freshness metadata, raw versus derived endpoints.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the developer page: dataset endpoints return data as published by the provider and can be requested by published time, which lets a client retrieve superseded values (earlier forecasts) or backfill an archive. This is the nearest public equivalent of Adele's as_of query. A metadata endpoint datasets/METADATA/latest gives the latest publish time of every dataset in one call (cheap freshness check: Adele could expose the same in 'adele list'). Endpoints are split into dataset (raw), opinionated (derived, e.g. /forecast/generation/wind/latest), stream (JSON, no row limit), summary and reference (standing data). No API key. Formats CSV, XML, JSON. Exact field names publishTime/settlementDate seen only in third-party listings of the OpenAPI spec, not on the page I read.
projects.status: Proprietary service, free, governed by BMRS Data Licence Terms (text not read). Active.

projects.name: Energi Data Service (Energinet, Denmark)
projects.what: Danish TSO's open data API: one generic endpoint per dataset plus a metadata endpoint.
projects.overlap: HTTP API design, dataset descriptor content, half-open time ranges.
projects.takeaways: Verified: data at api.energidataservice.dk/dataset/{name} with start (included) and end (excluded), columns, filter (JSON, equality only), sort, offset, limit; relative times (now, StartOfDay) with ISO 8601 offsets (startOffset=-PT15M). Metadata at /meta/dataset/{name}: I read the Elspotprices descriptor. Top-level keys include updateFrequency, resolution ('1 hour (PT1H)'), dataFrom, comment, caution, active, lastMetadataUpdate; per column: dbColumn, dataType, unit ('EUR per MWh'), description, comment, example, primaryKeyIndex, validationRules. Design points for Adele: a 'caution' text and an 'active' flag per dataset (Elspotprices is frozen and its description points to the successor dataset), one example value per column, primary key order in the descriptor. Counter-example: every dataset carries both HourUTC and HourDK and the API parameters use Danish local time; Adele's UTC-only rule avoids this. Rate limit guidance: one request per update period, HTTP 429 beyond; the docs tell vendors to download and serve the data themselves.
projects.status: Free, no authentication. License not in the metadata (not checked). Active.

projects.name: Energy-Charts API (Fraunhofer ISE)
projects.what: JSON API for European generation, load, prices, cross-border flows and forecasts, derived from ENTSO-E, SMARD and exchanges.
projects.overlap: Candidate upstream source for Adele fetchers; licensing per dataset and zone.
projects.takeaways: Verified in openapi.json: API version 2.0 (v2 dated 2026-07-20, v1 kept unchanged), a /v2 catalog endpoint that lists all endpoints, /v2/price?bzn=..., /v2/public_power, /v2/cbet, /v2/cbpf, forecasts by forecast_type (current, intraday, day-ahead, week-ahead). Rate limits are low: default 2 requests per minute per IP and endpoint, with Retry-After on 429, so it suits a server-side fetcher with a cache and not direct use by agents. License differs by zone: prices for AT, BE, CH, CZ, DE-LU, DK1, DK2, FR, HU, IT-North, NL, NO2, PL, SE4, SI are CC BY 4.0 (from SMARD); prices for all other zones are restricted to private and internal use. Consequence for Adele: the descriptor needs a license and a redistribution note per dataset, possibly per zone. Forecast type as a dimension is a reminder that 'forecast horizon' is a third time notion beside delivery and knowledge time.
projects.status: Hosted service, not open source. Active (v1.6 on 2026-06-26, v2 on 2026-07-20).

projects.name: Electricity Maps parsers (electricitymaps-contrib)
projects.what: Open repository of Python parsers that fetch and standardize production, consumption, price and exchange data per zone, worldwide.
projects.overlap: Scheduled fetchers and normalization; per-zone configuration.
projects.takeaways: Verified: parser kinds are production, consumption, price, production per unit, exchange, and four forecast kinds; static information is in yaml files under config/zones and config/exchanges (which parser to use per zone and data kind, capacities, fallbacks); 'uv run test_parser ZONE_KEY' runs one parser by hand. Useful pattern for Adele: yaml that maps dataset to fetcher function, and a CLI command to run one fetcher in isolation. The repo holds only the parsers: storage, revisions and the API are in the closed commercial product. Function signatures and validation rules not verified (wiki pages did not load).
projects.status: AGPL-3.0 since v1.5.0 (earlier contributions MIT), so copying code into Adele has license consequences. 6,922 commits, 4.0k stars; last commit date not checked.

projects.name: Open Power System Data (time series package)
projects.what: Academic project that compiled European load, wind, solar and price time series into versioned data packages.
projects.overlap: Frictionless datapackage for European electricity time series; versioning by date.
projects.takeaways: Verified: each release is labelled by date (YYYY-MM-DD) with its own DOI, and a 'latest' URL points to the newest; files in CSV (single index, multi index, stacked), XLSX and SQLite with datapackage.json and README; two timestamp columns (utc_timestamp, cet_cest_timestamp) marking the start of the period; wide layout with column names such as DE_LU_wind_onshore_generation_actual and AT_load_actual_entsoe_transparency (zone, variable, source encoded in the name). Lesson for Adele: the wide layout forces a new column for each zone or source, which is a schema change; Adele's long grain (bidding_zone, delivery_start) avoids that. The 'stacked' variant is the equivalent of the long form. Pipeline was Jupyter notebooks (GitHub repo Open-Power-System-Data/time_series, MIT).
projects.status: Effectively dormant: the latest time series version is 2020-10-06, data ends mid-2020. Repo not archived. Do not use as a source.

projects.name: SMARD (Bundesnetzagentur) and the bundesAPI description
projects.what: German regulator's market data portal; its undocumented JSON backend is described by the community project bundesAPI.
projects.overlap: Upstream source; pattern for static partitioned files with an index.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the bundesAPI page: two URL patterns, an index https://www.smard.de/app/chart_data/{filter}/{region}/index_{resolution}.json that lists the available start timestamps (epoch milliseconds), and data files {filter}_{region}_{resolution}_{timestamp}.json. Numeric filter ids (410 = load, 4068 = photovoltaic, ...), regions DE, AT, LU, DE-LU, control areas. The design is 'static chunk files plus an index file', with no query server. Adele's pull command needs the same thing: a manifest of partitions per dataset that the client compares with its local copy. Weak points to avoid: opaque numeric ids, no units or descriptions in the payload. Data license CC BY 4.0 (seen in the Energy-Charts spec, which attributes price data to 'Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de'; not read on smard.de).
projects.status: Official portal active; the API description is unofficial (community repo, 50 commits, license and last activity not checked). Search results mention notices about data gaps on smard.de (not read).

projects.name: Ember (API and European wholesale price dataset)
projects.what: Think tank that publishes cleaned electricity data: an API for yearly and monthly generation, demand, emissions, and CSV files of European day-ahead prices.
projects.overlap: Republishing of ENTSO-E day-ahead prices; API key per user by email.
projects.takeaways: Verified: API docs at https://api.ember-energy.org/v1/docs, key obtained by email signup; API covers only yearly and monthly data (not hourly). The European wholesale price dataset (https://ember-energy.org/data/european-wholesale-electricity-price-data/) offers hourly (zip, one file per country plus a compiled file), daily and monthly CSV; sources ENTSO-E, EMR, SEMOpx; last updated 12 Nov 2026; missing values are interpolated and mixed 15-minute and 60-minute markets are averaged. This is a counter-example for Adele: silent interpolation and aggregation to country level remove the information that a trading or forecasting user needs. It can serve as a cross-check for Adele's own price series. No machine-readable descriptor found.
projects.status: CC-BY-4.0. Active. Rate limits not stated.

projects.name: Swissgrid grid data files
projects.what: Swiss TSO publishes downloadable files: yearly 'Energy Statistic Switzerland' workbooks (15-minute data), Control Area Balance, Total System Imbalance.
projects.overlap: Upstream source with revisions and unstable URLs; test case for fetchers and revision policy.
projects.takeaways: Verified: Energy Statistic is XLSX for 2020 to 2026 and XLS for 2009 to 2019, published on the 15th working day after month end, corrected monthly, and considered reliable only 6 months after publication (a clear case for append-only with fetched_at). Control Area Balance and Total System Imbalance are CSV/XLSX at 15-minute resolution, refreshed during the day. File URLs have the form https://www.swissgrid.ch/dam/jcr:<UUID>/<filename>, and the UUID cannot be predicted, so a fetcher must scrape the page for links. No API, no explicit open license on the page (the Swiss catalogue by SFOE also marks Swissgrid's open-data status as 'unknown'). The descriptor needs fields for 'provisional until' and for license 'unknown'.
projects.status: Official, active. License not stated.

projects.name: BFE energiedashboard.ch datasets on opendata.swiss and the SFOE data catalogue
projects.what: The Swiss Federal Office of Energy publishes the CSV files behind its energy dashboard on opendata.swiss (CKAN, DCAT-AP CH), and maintains a markdown catalogue of about 40 Swiss open energy datasets.
projects.overlap: Swiss upstream sources; human-readable catalog format.
projects.takeaways: Verified in the SFOE repo: each dataset entry is a short description plus a table with scope, data category (survey, statistical aggregation, model, potential analysis), level of detail, format, access link, documentation link, open data yes/no/unknown, update interval, owner, contact. The 'data category' field (measured versus modelled versus estimated) is absent from the Adele spec and matters for series such as the model-based national consumption estimate. From search results only: BFE datasets named 'energiedashboard.ch: ...' (Swissgrid consumption, production, import/export, gas storage) exist on opendata.swiss as CSV, some hosted on uvek-gis.admin.ch, and a hackathon project built an API over them. I could not open the opendata.swiss pages (HTTP 403), so update frequency and terms are not verified.
projects.status: SFOE repo: 16 commits, no license shown, last activity not checked. opendata.swiss dataset pages not verified (403).

projects.name: gridstatus (open-source library) and Grid Status hosted API
projects.what: Python library that fetches market data from North American ISOs and the EIA, with a separate commercial hosted API.
projects.overlap: Fetchers; split between raw fetch library and normalized hosted layer.
projects.takeaways: Verified in the README: the library returns minimally processed data with source-specific columns, and the README says column names vary by method and source. The hosted API is where the consistent column names, timestamp formats, DST handling, historical archive and server-side filters are provided. This is the same split as Adele (fetchers versus normalized store) and confirms that the normalization layer is the costly part. US only, so no reuse for ENTSO-E. For European fetchers the search found entsoe-py (EnergieID), whose EntsoeFileClient reads the ENTSO-E File Library that replaced the SFTP service (seen in search results, not verified on ENTSO-E pages).
projects.status: BSD-3-Clause. 942 commits; release date not checked.

projects.name: Open Electricity (formerly OpenNEM, Australia)
projects.what: Open platform for Australian electricity market data with an API key per user and Python and TypeScript SDKs.
projects.overlap: API key per user, Python client that returns pandas or polars frames.
projects.takeaways: Verified: platform and client libraries are in beta; code MIT, data CC BY-NC 4.0 (code and data licensed separately, as in PUDL); docs pages have a 'Copy as Markdown' option and .md URLs appear in search results, which is a cheap way to make docs readable by agents. From search results only: the Python SDK has sync and async clients and exports to pandas or polars; the backend repo is opennem/opennem. Endpoints, units metadata and limits not read.

projects.name: Open Energy Platform (OEP)
projects.what: German research platform with a community database for energy scenario and model data, a REST API and the oemetadata standard.
projects.overlap: Catalog plus database plus API for energy data.
projects.takeaways: Verified only at a high level: web interface and REST API to read and write tables, metadata and scenario bundles; data described with oemetadata; upload wizard and a metadata builder tool. It targets researchers who upload scenario data (client writes, review badges), not scheduled republication of market data. Only its metadata standard is of use for Adele (see the oemetadata entry). Storage engine and versioning not verified.
projects.status: Active site; version, license of the platform code and release dates not checked.

projects.name: entsoe-py (EnergieID)
projects.what: Python client for the ENTSO-E Transparency Platform REST API, with a raw client (XML) and a pandas client that parses to Series/DataFrame.
projects.overlap: Server fetchers for the ENTSO-E datasets; conventions for bidding zone codes, time zones and resolution.
projects.takeaways: Verified in README and source (entsoe/entsoe.py, entsoe/mappings.py). (1) start/end must be tz-aware pd.Timestamp, otherwise exception; they are converted to UTC, rounded to the hour and sent as YYYYMMDDhh00. (2) Results are converted to the LOCAL time zone of the area (df.tz_convert(area.tz)), labels mark period start. Adele must convert back to UTC. (3) The end bound is NOT half-open: df.truncate(before=start, after=end) keeps the row that starts at `end`. A fetcher that chains windows will get duplicate rows at the boundaries, so deduplicate on the grain key. (4) Zones are an `Area` enum: short name (DE_LU, CH, IT_NORD, NO_2) --> EIC code ('10Y1001A1001A82H'), meaning, IANA tz. Good source for Adele's zone reference table (name, EIC, tz). (5) README states zone codes are valid only for certain periods (DE_AT_LU 2015-2018, DE_LU and AT from 2018). (6) Resolution changes inside one dataset: query_day_ahead_prices forces hourly before 2025-10-01 and 15 min after (constant QUARTER_MTU_SDAC_GOLIVE); the `resolution` argument is deprecated. (7) Release notes show repeated breakage after ENTSO-E changes (monthly_limited became required, IDA go-live redesign): a schema drift alert in Adele is justified.
projects.status: MIT. Latest release V0.8.1 dated '04 Sep' on the releases page (year not shown, could not confirm it is 2026); previous v0.8.0 '14 Apr'. 500 commits. PyPI page could not be loaded.

projects.name: gridstatus.io hosted API + gridstatusio client
projects.what: Commercial hosted API (free tier) over North American ISO data, with a dataset catalog, a metadata endpoint per dataset and a Python client (gridstatusio, BSD-3).
projects.overlap: Closest prior art for the catalog descriptor, the list/describe/query client, the knowledge time axis (publish time) and API keys.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the docs. Metadata fields per dataset: id, name, description, earliest_available_time_utc, latest_available_time_utc, source, source_url, last_checked_time_utc, primary_key_columns, publish_time_column, time_index_column, subseries_index_column, all_columns (name, type, is_numeric, is_datetime), number_of_rows_approximate, data_frequency, publication_frequency, status (active | deprecated | retired). No units per column and no ETA of next refresh: Adele's descriptor is richer on both. Worth copying: naming the time index column and the publish time column in the descriptor, primary_key_columns as machine-readable grain, a dataset lifecycle status separate from fetch status. Time: all datetimes returned in UTC by default; start_time inclusive, end_time excluded (half-open, same as Adele); input without offset is assumed UTC; filters apply only to time_index_column. Bitemporal: publish_time=latest (for each interval start, the record with the most recent publish time), publish_time=latest_before:<offset>, and publish_time_start/publish_time_end. This is the same idea as Adele's as_of. Client: list_datasets(), get_dataset(dataset, start, end, limit), get_dataset_metadata(), get_api_usage(); returns pandas, polars or dicts. Docs publish llms.txt and llms-full.txt for agents. Column names interval_start_utc / interval_end_utc were NOT confirmed on the pages fetched.
projects.status: Hosted service, not self-hostable. gridstatusio client BSD-3-Clause, version not checked. Free plan 500,000 rows per month (per client README).

projects.name: gridstatus (open-source library)
projects.what: Python library with one class per North American ISO (CAISO, ERCOT, PJM, MISO, SPP, NYISO, ISO-NE, IESO, AESO) plus EIA, returning pandas DataFrames.
projects.overlap: Uniform interface over heterogeneous market sources; conventions for time columns.
projects.takeaways: Verified on README: returns DataFrames with timezone-aware columns; date inputs are interpreted in the ISO's own local timezone (opposite of the hosted API, which assumes UTC); README says 'Use fixed dates for reproducible results' and 'Filtering capabilities vary by source'. Methods are now named per dataset and market interval (get_lmp_real_time_5_min_by_location, get_lmp_day_ahead_hourly) and not one generic get_lmp with parameters: the resolution and market are part of the dataset identity. This supports Adele's choice of one descriptor per dataset with a fixed grain. No European coverage, so no reuse as fetcher. The 'Interval Start / Interval End / Publish Time' column convention is from memory and was not verified (docs changelog returned 403).
projects.status: BSD-3-Clause. Version 0.37.0 released 2026-10-23 per PyPI (page loaded once). Actively maintained.

projects.name: Energy Quantified Python client
projects.what: Open-source client (Apache 2.0) for the commercial Energy Quantified API. Its data model for 'curves' is the most explicit vocabulary found for market time series.
projects.overlap: Vocabulary for the adele: extension block: resolution, units, revision policy, forecast instances.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the terminology page. (1) Resolution = frequency + time zone. Frequencies use ISO 8601 durations: P1Y, P3M, P1M, P1W, P1D, PT1H, PT30M, PT15M, PT10M, PT5M, PT1M, plus SEASON and NONE (irregular, tick data). Point for Adele: P1D and P1M have no fixed length in UTC; a daily value is a day in a local zone (CET, or the gas day starting 06:00 CET), so the descriptor needs a time zone next to the resolution for calendar frequencies. (2) Each curve declares a curve_type that tells which operation loads it: TIMESERIES, SCENARIO_TIMESERIES, INSTANCE, PERIODS, PERIOD_INSTANCES, OHLC, TRADES, PPA. INSTANCE = a forecast identified by (issued datetime, tag such as 'ec'). This maps to Adele's revision policy: overwrite ~ TIMESERIES, append-only with fetched_at ~ INSTANCE, and 'issued' is a source-side knowledge time that differs from fetched_at. (3) PERIODS = begin/end ranges with a value (outages, capacities): tabular data that does not fit 'one row per delivery_start' at fixed resolution. (4) Closed unit list: MW, MWh, MWh/h, EUR, etc. (5) Half-open intervals are implied by examples (2020-01-01 to 2020-01-05 = 4 days), not stated.
projects.status: Apache 2.0 (verified on GitHub README). Release version and date not checked. Requires a paid API subscription.

projects.name: ClariGrid
projects.what: New Python SDK that normalises European and US energy data from many public providers (Energy-Charts, SMARD, Elia, ENTSO-E, EIA, CAISO, NYISO, weather sources) to pandas DataFrames, with a local Parquet cache.
projects.overlap: Same goal as Adele's normalisation layer and local cache, done on the client side without a server or catalog.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the repo README. Conventions: tz-aware DatetimeIndex named utc_time; data fetched and cached in UTC, conversion only on output (cg.set_timezone()). Zones follow ENTSO-E names (BE, DE_LU, FR) for Europe and EIA balancing authority codes for the US, with aliases (DE --> DE_LU). Units are encoded in column names (load_mw, price_mwh, flow_kwh_d, frequency_hz, *_pct), currency in df.attrs. Sign convention stated for cross-border flows (imports positive). Parquet cache under ~/.clarigrid/cache keyed by provider, dataset, zone, date range; historical data cached forever, live data expires after 1 hour. Lessons for Adele: (a) a unit suffix in the column name survives any SQL query, whereas a unit in the descriptor is lost once the agent has the DataFrame, so consider both; (b) sign conventions belong in the field description; (c) 'cache forever' is wrong for datasets with revisions, which Adele's revision policy handles. Listed on MCP directories by a search result, but the README does not mention MCP.
projects.status: Apache 2.0, copyright 2026. 44 commits, 3 stars, no releases shown: very young, single author. Not suitable as a dependency. PyPI page could not be loaded.

projects.name: PUDL (Catalyst Cooperative)
projects.what: Pipeline that cleans and integrates US public energy datasets (EIA, FERC, EPA) and publishes them as Parquet files and a DuckDB database, rebuilt nightly.
projects.overlap: Server design (normalise to Parquet, DuckDB), authored metadata in git, units per field, never changing data silently.
projects.takeaways: Verified on README and docs. Outputs: Parquet as primary format, plus pudl.duckdb; pudl.sqlite is deprecated and stops in 2027. Nightly builds with validation tests before publication. Metadata is authored in code: FIELD_METADATA keyed by field name (type, description, optional unit, constraints enum/pattern) so that fields with the same name share one definition across tables, with overrides per resource. Units are validated against a pint UnitRegistry, compound units written 'USD / MWh'. Resources declare primary_key (non-null, tested for uniqueness when written) and foreign keys. Schemas are enforced with Pandera. Raw input archives on Zenodo are Frictionless data packages. EIA-930 hourly data is stored in UTC, and a codes table gives the reporting time zone per balancing authority for re-localisation. For Adele: a shared field dictionary (delivery_start, bidding_zone, fetched_at defined once), a uniqueness test of the grain at every write, and a registry for unit strings.
projects.status: Software MIT, data CC-BY-4.0. 11,292 commits, nightly builds, active in 2026. Latest release version not checked. US data only.

projects.name: jao-py
projects.what: Python client for the JAO (Joint Allocation Office) publication tools: flow-based capacity data for Core day-ahead, Core intraday, Nordic and Italy North.
projects.overlap: Server fetcher for JAO datasets if they are among the dozen.
projects.takeaways: Verified on README: separate pandas clients per region (JaoPublicationToolPandasClient for Core DA from business day 2022-06-09, ...PandasIntraDay with versions a to d, ...PandasNordics from 2024-10-30, ...PandasItalyNorth), legacy CWE clients deprecated. Data is organised by 'business day', a local calendar day (CET), not a UTC interval: a fetcher must map a business day to 23, 24 or 25 hours of UTC. Coverage start dates differ per market version, which is the kind of fact Adele's coverage field must carry. Time zone handling of inputs and outputs is not documented in the README (not verified). Same author also contributes to entsoe-py.
projects.status: MIT. Latest release V0.8.7 dated '03 Nov' (year not shown on the page; presumably 2026, not confirmed).

projects.name: Open Power System Data - time series package
projects.what: Research data package with European load, wind, solar and price time series, published as CSV, XLSX and SQLite with a Frictionless datapackage.json.
projects.overlap: Catalog format: the main existing example of electricity time series described with a Frictionless Data Package.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the package page. One file per resolution (time_series_15min, _30min, _60min), never mixed. With a local timezone, 'Daylight saving time (DST) changes within the requested range are ignored' and the docs recommend unixtime: evidence that local time output causes errors, UTC only is right. Every response carries a units object (hourly_units) with one unit per selected variable: units travel with the data, not only in the docs. 15-minutely data is native only in Central Europe and North America and is interpolated from hourly elsewhere, so a nominal resolution can hide a coarser native resolution (Adele could record 'native_resolution' when a source upsamples). Past forecasts 'as issued' are served by separate APIs (Historical Forecast, Previous Model Runs, Single Runs), not by a parameter of the main endpoint.

results.angle_summary:
No library found is reusable as a whole: they are clients of one source (entsoe-py, jao-py: reuse as fetchers) or hosted services (gridstatus.io, Energy Quantified). None combines self-hosted Parquet, a descriptor per dataset and an agent skill.

Conventions diverge, which confirms Adele's UTC and half-open rule: entsoe-py returns local time of the zone and keeps the row that starts at `end` (inclusive); gridstatus.io is UTC and end-exclusive; JAO and Elexon key data by local business day or settlement period.

Challenges to the spec:
1. Resolution is not constant per dataset (day-ahead prices: 60 min --> 15 min on 2025-10-01). Store delivery_end per row, or resolution with validity periods.
2. Bidding zone codes have validity periods (DE_AT_LU --> DE_LU). Needs a zone reference table (name, EIC, tz, valid_from/to).
3. Daily and monthly resolutions need a time zone (EQ: resolution = frequency + tz).
4. Source publish time ("issued") differs from fetched_at; gridstatus.io exposes publish_time_column in metadata.
5. Outage-like "period" data does not fit a fixed grain.

No serious project in this angle does what Adele plans (local Parquet sync, bitemporal as_of, schema-drift alerts). Almost all are thin MCP wrappers: one tool per upstream endpoint, live calls, units only in tool descriptions, no coverage or freshness metadata. Vendors named in the brief: only Modo Energy (official MCP, June 2026) and Kpler (not power) verified. Nothing found for Montel, Volue, Energy Quantified, Amperon; Enverus, gridstatus and Electricity Maps only have third-party wrappers. Best ideas to copy: (1) eptr2's CLI `list | search | describe | schema` plus bundled skills and `install-skills` (closest match to Adele's CLI + skill design, confirms the no-MCP choice); (2) Grid Status dataset metadata fields (publication_frequency, publish_time_column, primary_key_columns, status enum); (3) cyanheads EIA server: browse/describe/search/query plus DuckDB staging, errors with a recovery hint; (4) Energy Aspects `release_date` (as_of) and schema resources. Challenge to the spec: add `adele search`, and a machine-readable full schema dump.

projects.name: eptr2 (Tideseed / Robokami)
projects.what: Unofficial Python client for the Turkish EPIAS transparency platform (234 endpoints) that ships a CLI, an MCP server with 18 tools, 7 bundled agent skills and an AGENTS.md.
projects.overlap: Client CLI (list / describe), SKILL.md with progressive disclosure, catalog discovery without credentials, machine-readable schema.
projects.takeaways: Closest design to Adele that I found. Verified on the repo page: `eptr2 list`, `eptr2 search`, `eptr2 describe` work without credentials; `describe` returns parameters, method, path, description; `eptr2 schema --stdout` dumps a machine-readable description of all 234 endpoints (also committed as eptr2_api_schema.json); `eptr2 install-skills` copies the skills to project or user scope (`--client claude`); `eptr2 mcp-config --client <name>` writes the MCP config; `strict_params=True` raises on unknown parameters (otherwise a misspelled filter is dropped with a warning and the query silently widens). Skills are split by domain (prices, consumption, generation, imbalance, market operations, API discovery, typed wrappers), one SKILL.md per folder with trigger keywords and sample queries (docs: https://tideseed.github.io/eptr2/ai-integration/agent-skills). Ideas for Adele: add `adele search`, add `adele install-skill`, add a full schema dump command, fail loudly on unknown filters. No Parquet store, no freshness or coverage metadata, no bitemporal handling.

projects.name: Grid Status (gridstatus.io) API and docs
projects.what: Commercial hosted API over 455+ normalized datasets from US ISOs, with a dataset catalog and a per-dataset metadata endpoint. No official MCP server found.
projects.overlap: Catalog descriptor fields, freshness and publish time, incremental sync, agent-readable docs.
projects.takeaways: Best model for Adele's server-computed catalog fields. Verified on https://docs.gridstatus.io/developers/api-reference/dataset-metadata.md : `GET /v1/datasets/{dataset_id}` returns id, name, description, earliest_available_time_utc, latest_available_time_utc, source, source_url, data_frequency, publication_frequency, publish_time_column, last_checked_time_utc, primary_key_columns, time_index_column, subseries_index_column, all_columns (name, type, is_numeric, is_datetime), number_of_rows_approximate, status (active / deprecated / retired). Mapping to Adele: primary_key_columns = grain, publish_time_column = knowledge time axis, data_frequency vs publication_frequency = resolution vs refresh, status enum includes deprecated. No units per column and no ETA of next refresh (Adele would add both). The docs index lists a recipe "Backfill and Incrementally Sync a Dataset" (high-watermark sync), "Data Freshness Monitoring", "Dataset Audit", "Dataset Updates", "Bulk CSV Downloads" (added 2026-02-09), a changelog entry that adds the `_utc` suffix to columns, llms.txt, and a `.md` version of every docs page. No MCP is mentioned in the official docs.

projects.name: cyanheads/eia-energy-mcp-server
projects.what: Open-source MCP server over the US EIA API v2 with discovery tools and a DuckDB staging area where the agent runs SQL on fetched results.
projects.overlap: list / describe / search / query pattern, DuckDB SQL for agents, shape of responses and errors.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the listing page: 6 tools: eia_browse_routes, eia_describe_route (facets, valid values, data columns, frequencies, date range), eia_search_routes (fuzzy search over names, descriptions, column names, facet values), eia_query_route, eia_dataframe_describe, eia_dataframe_query. `stage: true` puts up to 25,000 rows (max 250,000) in DuckDB; the query tool accepts one read-only SELECT and rejects writes, file reads and access to the system catalog; staged frames expire after 24 h. Response design to copy in the Adele CLI: a truncated response reports the count against the cap and a `notice` that names the next call; errors carry a `reason` and a `recovery` hint; describe says explicitly when a column has no unit; the date range is stated as valid for the default frequency only. Confirms that "SQL through DuckDB" is a good interface for agents, and that the query endpoint needs a SQL guard (single SELECT, no file reads).

results.angle_summary: All projects converge on three steps: list --> describe --> free SQL, with the SQL engine read-only by default and results capped (MotherDuck local: 1024 rows / 50,000 chars; lacon: 50 rows; cyanheads: 10,000 rows). This matches adele list | describe | query. Two vendors that started with MCP later added SKILL.md catalogs (MotherDuck, Data Commons), and Hugging Face and DuckDB ship CLI + skill. This supports the CLI + skill choice. Challenges to the spec: (1) add explicit row and character caps and a visible truncation marker to `adele query`; (2) add a "describe before query" rule and DuckDB dialect hints to the skill; (3) consider a server-side "guide" text per dataset (domain notes), as MotherDuck Guides and boettiger-lab prompt files do; (4) restrict the server DuckDB (no ATTACH, INSTALL, SET, local files). No project found covers freshness, ETA of next refresh, units or bitemporal queries: this part of Adele has no prior art in this angle.

projects.name: MotherDuck Agent Skills
projects.what: Open-source catalog of 17 SKILL.md skills (connect, explore, query, duckdb-sql, plus workflow and use-case skills) that teach coding agents to use MotherDuck/DuckDB. Announced at https://motherduck.com/blog/motherduck-agent-skills/

The agent sees only names and descriptions at start ("lazy loading"). Three layers: utility, workflow, use-case. Reported lessons: MCP alone gives tools but not the preferred path; without guidance agents write PostgreSQL-flavoured SQL, invent tables; skills should be decision frameworks, not copies of the docs; a validation script runs queries before building on them. Defaults they teach: DuckDB SQL, fully qualified table names, Parquet over CSV. Remote server has "Guide tools": markdown documents with metric definitions and domain context, stored server-side. For Adele: row and character caps on `adele query`; lock the server DuckDB; a per-dataset notes field comparable to Guides.

Curated markdown files are loaded at start: query-optimization.md and h3-guide.md are injected verbatim into the description of the query tool; query-setup.md runs as SQL in every fresh connection. Bearer token on every route. For Adele: a standard catalog format as the single source for describe (they use STAC, Adele uses Frictionless); a setup SQL per connection (e.g. views per dataset); memory and spill guards on a single box. The public hosted endpoint is offline (NRP closed public access), which is an argument for self-hosting.

results.angle_summary: The evidence supports CLI + SKILL.md for Adele's users (coding agents with a shell), but not as a general rule. Controlled evals (Scale Labs, Arize) find that correctness is about equal between MCP and CLI on frontier models; the differences are in cost, turns and composition, and they depend on the harness. Claude Code now defers MCP tool definitions by default, so the argument "MCP fills the context" is weaker than in 2025. Challenge to the spec: (1) a thin MCP wrapper is only needed for chat clients without a shell; (2) write a short opinionated skill, with `adele describe` as the source of truth, not a copy of the catalog; (3) measured gains for SQL come from representative values, keys, and column descriptions (a few points each on BIRD), so 5 sample rows should be complemented by distinct values per categorical column; (4) no benchmark found measures units or grain: build a small eval of 10 to 20 questions.

projects.name: Vercel d0: "We removed 80% of our agent's tools"
projects.what: Blog post (Andrew Qu, 2025-12-22) on Vercel's internal text-to-SQL agent. The team replaced many specialised tools with bash access to a directory of semantic layer files (Cube; YAML, Markdown, JSON), plus SQL execution.
projects.overlap: Catalog as files that the agent explores with grep/cat; CLI + shell instead of a tool per operation; catalog quality as the precondition.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the page: 5 representative queries only; average time 274.8s --> 77.4s, tokens ~102k --> ~61k, steps ~12 --> ~7, success 4/5 --> 5/5. With n=5, the success difference (one query) is not evidence of better accuracy; the cost and time reductions are the credible part. The prose says 'a single tool' but the code sample lists ExecuteCommand and ExecuteSQL. The authors state that the approach 'only worked because' the semantic layer was already well documented, and that with poor naming it gives 'faster bad queries'. For Adele: after `adele pull`, also put the descriptors (yaml) on local disk so that the agent can grep them; this gives the same file exploration for free. Invest in the descriptors before the tooling.
projects.status: Blog post, fetched and verified 2025-12-22 version. Companion npm package bash-tool mentioned by secondary sources, not checked.

projects.name: Scale Labs: MCP vs CLI tool interfaces (benchmark)
projects.what: Controlled comparison (dated 2026-07-08) of MCP-only, CLI-only, both, and hybrid routing on 50 long agentic tasks in two enterprise-style environments (113 and 140 tools), with Opus 4.6/4.8 and GPT-5.4/5.5, at least 4 runs per task and condition.
projects.overlap: Direct evidence on the spec decision 'CLI + skill, no MCP'.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the page: on the latest models (Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5) all conditions perform similarly; CLI helped weaker models on the data-heavy environment (Opus 4.6: about 8.5% --> 17.7% task success) mainly by reducing errors of query construction and tool selection. Cost depends on the harness: Opus 4.8 under Claude Code was cheaper with MCP (16 turns, $2.84/run) than with CLI (42 turns, $3.52/run); GPT-5.5 was cheaper with CLI ($2.11 vs $3.51). CLI was 20 to 40% slower in wall-clock time. Important caveat stated by the authors: the CLI was exposed through a light skill that only points to `--help`, so the agent spent turns on command discovery. For Adele: put the 4 commands with one example each directly in SKILL.md so that the agent does not need `--help` round trips; this is the cost that the benchmark attributes to CLI. When both interfaces were offered, models almost always used MCP, so offering both without routing rules is the worst option.
projects.status: Blog post by Scale AI, fetched and verified. One number pair for Opus 4.6 on environment 1 was ambiguous in the extract.

projects.name: Arize: MCP vs CLI Skills eval
projects.what: Eval by Laurie Voss (May 2026): 25 GitHub tasks in 4 tiers, 5 runs each, Opus 4.6 in the Claude Agent SDK; arms: GitHub MCP server, a 2,187-line skill, a 341-line prescriptive skill, and bare Claude with a shell.
projects.overlap: Skill length and style; CLI + skill versus MCP for analysis tasks that need composition.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the page: correctness about equal across arms (baseline 0.845, MCP 0.834, short skill 0.833, long skill 0.826); these differences are too small to rank the arms with 25 tasks. On complex analysis tasks MCP cost more than 6 times as much and took about 5 times as long, because the agent left MCP and used bash to post-process JSON (tool fidelity 0.33). The short opinionated skill cost less than the long encyclopedic one. The authors note that for a well-known CLI (gh) the training data does much of the work, and that a proprietary CLI will need a skill or MCP. For Adele: `adele` is unknown to the model, so the skill is required; keep it in the range of a few hundred lines at most; analysis tasks (joins, aggregation over partitions) are exactly the composition case where shell + local DuckDB is cheaper.
projects.status: Vendor blog (Arize sells eval tooling), fetched and verified. A later update about Claude Code deferring MCP tools was reported by search but not present on the fetched page.

projects.name: Anthropic: Skill authoring best practices (docs)
projects.what: Official documentation on how to write a SKILL.md: frontmatter limits, progressive disclosure patterns, scripts, evaluation.
projects.overlap: The Adele SKILL.md and how to disclose a catalog of a dozen datasets progressively.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the page: name max 64 characters, description max 1,024 characters, written in third person, stating what the skill does and when to use it; SKILL.md body under 500 lines; references one level deep from SKILL.md (nested references get partially read with `head -100`); table of contents for reference files over 100 lines; only script output consumes tokens. The page contains an example that matches Adele closely: a 'bigquery-skill' with SKILL.md as navigation and one reference file per domain (finance.md, sales.md), plus grep hints. It also advises to build 3 evaluations before writing the skill, and to avoid time-sensitive information. For Adele: the skill must not embed coverage, freshness or status (they go stale); it should say 'run `adele describe <id>`'. A static one-line list of dataset ids with grain is acceptable; everything computed by the server stays behind the CLI.

projects.name: Anthropic engineering: Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills
projects.what: Engineering post (2025-10-16, updated 2025-12-18 when Agent Skills became an open standard) that defines the three levels of progressive disclosure.
projects.overlap: Skill design; portability of the SKILL.md format across agents.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the page: level 1 = name + description preloaded in the system prompt; level 2 = SKILL.md body read when relevant; level 3 = linked files read on demand; scripts are executed without loading them in context. No token figures on this page. Security note: skills should come from trusted sources (relevant because the Adele skill ships to team members with an API key). The mapping to Adele's CLI is direct: `list` = level 1 of the catalog, `describe` = level 2, sample rows and full field list = level 3. Design `adele list` output to be about one line per dataset (id, grain, resolution, coverage, status).

projects.name: Anthropic engineering: Code execution with MCP
projects.what: Engineering post (2025-11-04) on the two costs of direct MCP tool calls (definitions loaded upfront; intermediate results passing through the model) and on presenting tools as files that the agent explores.
projects.overlap: Rationale for `adele pull` + local DuckDB (data stays out of the context), and for `adele query` output limits.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the page: one example workflow went from about 150,000 to 2,000 tokens (98.7%); this is a single illustrative example, not a benchmark. The principle that matters for Adele is the second cost: result sets must not pass through the model. The page gives the example of filtering a 10,000-row sheet in code and showing 5 rows. For Adele: `adele query` should by default print a truncated preview with the row count and write the full result to a file (parquet/csv) when asked (`--out`), so that the agent continues in Python. A `search_tools`-like detail level (name only / name + description / full schema) maps to `adele list` versus `adele describe` versus `adele describe --full`. Caveat on the page: running agent code needs sandboxing.
projects.status: Official post, fetched and verified.

projects.name: Anthropic engineering: Writing effective tools for agents
projects.what: Engineering post (2025-09-11) with concrete rules for the output of tools used by agents; the rules apply equally to CLI output.
projects.overlap: Output design of `adele list | describe | query`, error messages, eval method.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the page: offer concise versus detailed response formats (example: 72 versus 206 tokens); Claude Code caps tool responses at 25,000 tokens by default; when truncating, tell the agent how to narrow the request; error messages should state the fix or show a correct input; return meaningful names instead of opaque ids; few consolidated tools beat many overlapping ones; small changes in descriptions have large effects, so evaluate with realistic tasks and read the transcripts. For Adele: errors of `adele query` should name the valid datasets/columns ('column price not found; columns: price_eur_mwh, ...') and a failed dataset status should be visible in the error of `query`, not only in `describe`.

projects.name: MotherDuck CLI (agent docs) and motherduckdb/agent-skills
projects.what: MotherDuck's CLI bundles DuckDB and is documented explicitly for agents; a separate MIT repository (https://github.com/motherduckdb/agent-skills) holds 21 skills in three layers (utility, workflow, use-case). MotherDuck also runs an MCP server.

Quote: 'MCP tools are remote calls: every result comes back through the model.' Concrete features worth copying: `-o json` / `--output csv` on query; failures print `{"success": false, "error": "..."}` with a non-zero exit code; token from an environment variable; a home directory variable so that parallel agents do not share state; `guide` subcommands that print agent instructions locally, without network, always in the version that matches the installed CLI. For Adele: an `adele guide` (or `adele skill`) command that prints the current SKILL.md solves the problem of a skill that drifts from the CLI version. The docs recommend read-only tokens for agents (Adele is read-only by design). The repository states: skills do not configure the connection; references are loaded only when needed; 'DuckDB SQL, not PostgreSQL SQL'.

projects.name: MotherDuck research: Query-log-informed schema descriptions and text-to-SQL
projects.what: Thesis at MotherDuck (supervised by Hannes Muehleisen and Till Doehmen) that measures how samples and auto-generated column descriptions change execution accuracy on BIRD-Dev and on a benchmark built from MotherDuck's own warehouse.
projects.overlap: Which catalog metadata measurably helps: sample rows and descriptions.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the page: BIRD-Dev, Gemini 2.5 Flash: schema only 34.8% --> schema + samples 42.2% (+7.4 points) --> + descriptions mined from query patterns 44.0%. Same for Qwen 2.5-32B: 20.2% --> 28.2% with samples, but descriptions lowered it to 22.4%. On the in-house benchmark (2,730+ columns) descriptions gave Gemini +16 points (36% --> 52%) and reduced Qwen by 10. Reading: sample rows are the most reliable single addition for both models; long descriptions help strong models and can harm small ones. The useful content of a description was exact value formats and common filter expressions. For Adele: this supports the 5 sample rows, and suggests adding per field the list of distinct values for low-cardinality columns (bidding zone codes, flow direction, resolution) and one or two canonical example queries per dataset. Caveats: one thesis, percentages on the in-house set are in steps that suggest a small number of questions (not stated), so the gaps on that set have wide uncertainty.
projects.status: Research page fetched and verified; publication date and author name not stated on the page.

projects.name: Synthetic SQL Column Descriptions and Their Impact on Text-to-SQL Performance (arXiv 2408.04691)
projects.what: Paper that builds gold column descriptions for BIRD-Dev and measures zero-shot execution accuracy of six models with no descriptions, the original BIRD descriptions, gold descriptions, and LLM-generated ones.
projects.overlap: Field descriptions in the Frictionless descriptor; who should write them.
projects.takeaways: Verified in Table 3 of the page: every model improves with descriptions. GPT-4o: 30.1% without, 31.3% with BIRD originals, 33.3% with gold, 36.8% with verbose descriptions generated by Qwen2. Gains from 2 to 12 points depending on the model. The verbose descriptions, which human annotators judged redundant, gave the best accuracy. With column names replaced by codes (A11, A12), descriptions gave 'over 20%' (figure only, exact values not read). Models describe self-evident columns well and domain-dependent columns badly, so the authors propose automatic generation for clear columns and expert input for ambiguous ones. For Adele: informative column names with the unit in the name (price_eur_mwh, delivery_start_utc) reduce the dependence on descriptions; the human effort should go to the domain-dependent fields (sign conventions of flows, which price, as_of semantics). Caveat: GPT-4o helped build the gold set, which may bias its results.
projects.status: arXiv HTML v4 fetched and verified (first 100k characters).

projects.name: CodeS (arXiv 2402.16347): ablation of prompt metadata
projects.what: Open-source text-to-SQL models (1B to 15B) with a prompt that contains column types, comments, representative values, primary/foreign keys; the paper has the cleanest ablation of each metadata component.
projects.overlap: Which descriptor fields are worth the tokens.
projects.takeaways: Verified in Table 9 (3-shot, BIRD execution accuracy, 15B model): full prompt 35.14%; without representative values 31.94% (-3.2); without primary/foreign keys 32.14% (-3.0); without the value retriever 33.31%; without comments 34.03% (-1.1); without column data types 35.66% (no loss). On Spider the effects are all within about 1.5 points. Reading: values and keys matter most, comments a little, data types almost nothing once values are shown. These are single runs on older and smaller models than the ones Adele's users will run, so the ranking is indicative and the sizes are not transferable. For Adele: the 'grain' line is the equivalent of a primary key and belongs in the first lines of `describe`; add join keys between datasets (which column matches bidding_zone in another dataset) since Adele has no declared foreign keys.
projects.status: arXiv HTML v1 fetched and verified (Table 9). Paper from 2024.

projects.name: Spider 2.0 (arXiv 2411.07763) and BIRD (arXiv 2305.03111)
projects.what: The two reference benchmarks for text-to-SQL. Spider 2.0 has 632 enterprise workflow problems on databases that often have over 1,000 columns; BIRD has 12,751 pairs on 95 databases with human-written 'evidence' hints.
projects.overlap: What makes real SQL tasks hard for agents: metadata search, dialect documentation, external knowledge.
projects.takeaways: Verified in the abstracts: on Spider 2.0 the best code agent (o1-preview based) solved 21.3%, against 91.2% on Spider 1.0 and 73.0% on BIRD; the paper attributes the difficulty to searching metadata, consulting dialect documentation and reading project code. BIRD's abstract states that experiments show 'the significance of database values' for correct SQL. The SEED paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07423) states that models degrade markedly without BIRD's evidence and that the evidence is sometimes missing or wrong; exact drop not verified. Not found: any ablation in these benchmarks that isolates units, grain, or freshness metadata. Consequence for Adele: the claim that units and grain help is plausible but unmeasured; a dozen narrow tables is far from the Spider 2.0 regime, so schema retrieval is not Adele's problem, semantic ambiguity (which price, which time axis) is. A short DuckDB dialect note in the skill (time_bucket, ASOF JOIN, QUALIFY, interval arithmetic in UTC) addresses the 'dialect documentation' difficulty.
projects.status: Abstracts fetched and verified. Current leaderboard state (2026) not checked. Per-component ablations for Spider 2.0 not found.

projects.name: dbt Labs: Semantic Layer vs Text-to-SQL, 2026 benchmark, and dbt-agent-skills
projects.what: Blog post (2026-04-07) that reruns an 11-question benchmark on a 15-table insurance schema, 20 runs per question, comparing free text-to-SQL with queries through the dbt Semantic Layer. dbt also publishes skills (https://github.com/dbt-labs/dbt-agent-skills, Apache-2.0).
projects.overlap: Raw DuckDB SQL (`adele query`) versus governed metric definitions; effect of data modelling on agent accuracy.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the page: on the raw 3NF schema with DDL only, text-to-SQL went from 32.7% (GPT-4, 2023) to 64.5% (Sonnet 4.6 and GPT-5.3 Codex); after adding 3 denormalised models, text-to-SQL reached 90.0% (Sonnet 4.6) and 84.1% (GPT-5.3 Codex), the semantic layer 98.2% and 100%. Only 11 questions, one dataset, vendor-run: the direction is credible, the exact gaps are not. Two transferable points: (1) wide, denormalised, well-named tables raised text-to-SQL by about 25 points, more than any change of model; Adele's 'normalise every source to one tidy Parquet table with explicit grain' is this lever; (2) the failure types differ: text-to-SQL returns a wrong number without error, the semantic layer refuses. A semantic layer is too heavy for Adele, but a few named DuckDB views or macros for the error-prone operations (as_of filtering, resampling 15 min --> 1 h) give part of the benefit. The skills repo has an evals directory with an A/B tool to compare skill variants and uses gerund names (running-dbt-commands).

projects.name: Justin Poehnelt: Rewrite your CLI for AI agents (Google Workspace CLI lessons)
projects.what: Blog post (2026-03-04) with design principles for a CLI whose main user is an agent, drawn from the Google Workspace CLI (gws).

Dry-run and sanitisation matter less since Adele is read-only and the data is numeric.

results.angle_summary: No standard covers all of Adele's needs, so Frictionless Data Package v2 plus an "adele:" block is a defensible base. I verified that v2 has primaryKey but no unit, temporal coverage, update frequency or freshness, and no naming rule for custom properties. Challenge 1: declare the "adele:" block as a real v2 extension (a JSON Schema profile referenced by $schema) so that frictionless-py validates it. Challenge 2: do not invent field names. Borrow from oemetadata (unit per field, timeseries start/end/resolution/alignment/aggregationType, same domain, also Frictionless-based), from ODCS (slaProperties: frequency, latency, cron schedule; dataGranularityDescription) and from dbt (warn_after/error_after). Challenge 3: ODCS + datacontract-cli is the only stack with ready drift and breaking-change tooling on DuckDB/Parquet. Consider generating ODCS from the descriptor for those checks. Croissant, CSVW, DCAT and schema.org are export targets only. DuckLake could replace hand-built as_of logic.

projects.name: Frictionless Data Package v2 (Table Schema) + frictionless-py
projects.what: The JSON/YAML descriptor standard that Adele already plans to use: package, resource, table schema. frictionless-py is the reference Python library.
projects.overlap: Catalog descriptor (fields, types, primary key, sample values), validation of descriptors.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the spec pages: Table Schema has primaryKey, uniqueKeys, foreignKeys, missingValues, and per field name/title/description/example/type/format/constraints/categories/rdfType. It has NO unit property (a field 'MAY contain any number of other properties'), and the package level has NO temporal coverage, update frequency or freshness (only 'created', 'version', 'sources'). So units, grain text, coverage, refresh and revision policy must all be custom. The extensions page (https://datapackage.org/standard/extensions/) says an extension is a JSON Schema profile referenced by $schema that must include the default profile; it gives no naming rule for custom properties (no colon prefix convention; its example adds an unprefixed property). Recommendation: publish an Adele profile (JSON Schema) so that 'adele:' fields and per-field 'unit' are validated, not free text. Known extensions listed: Camera Trap DP, Fiscal DP. uniqueKeys/primaryKey can carry the grain in machine-readable form; keep the sentence 'one row per (...)' as an extra.
projects.status: Spec v2.0 released 2024-06-26 (search result, okfn blog); spec page last updated Aug 25, 2026. frictionless-py: MIT, 856 stars, PyPI 5.21.0 released 2026-10-15 (5.20.0 on 2026-10-08), extras include duckdb, parquet, pandas, sql, excel. projects.name: oemetadata (Open Energy Platform)
projects.what: Metadata standard for energy datasets, built on Frictionless Data Package, used by the Open Energy Platform. Nested JSON with schema, template and example.
projects.overlap: Units per field, temporal coverage and resolution of time series, primary key, sources and licenses. Same domain (energy) and same base standard as Adele.
projects.takeaways: Verified in metadata_key_description.md (v2.0): per-field 'unit' (example 'MW', null if not applicable), 'nullable', 'isAbout' and 'valueReference' (links to the Open Energy Ontology); a 'temporal' block with 'referenceDate' and 'timeseries[]' holding 'start', 'end', 'resolutionValue', 'resolutionUnit', 'alignment' (example 'left') and 'aggregationType' (example 'current'); 'primaryKey' and 'foreignKeys' in Frictionless form. Adele should copy 'alignment' and 'aggregationType': they state whether a 15-min value is stamped at the start of the interval and whether it is an average, a sum or an instantaneous value, which the Adele spec does not yet say. Adele's single ISO 8601 resolution string (PT15M) is cleaner than the value/unit pair. Nothing for update frequency, freshness or revisions. Reusing the key names would make an export to the Open Energy Platform cheap.

projects.name: Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS, Bitol / Linux Foundation)
projects.what: YAML standard for data contracts: schema, data quality rules, SLA, servers, team, pricing. Documented up to v3.2.0.
projects.overlap: Refresh frequency, freshness SLA, grain, primary key, partitioning, quality rules, sample values.
projects.takeaways: Verified: the SLA section defines slaProperties entries with 'property' (recommended values: availability, throughput, errorRate, generalAvailability, endOfSupport, endOfLife, retention, frequency, latency, timeToDetect, timeToNotify, timeToRepair), 'value', 'valueExt', 'unit' (d, y...), 'element' (object.column that the SLA is measured on), 'driver', 'scheduler' (e.g. cron) and 'schedule' (cron string). This is the richest vocabulary found for 'refresh every 15 min, at most N late, measured on column X' and for computing the ETA of the next refresh from a cron string. The schema section has 'primaryKey' + 'primaryKeyPosition', 'partitioned' + 'partitionKeyPosition', 'logicalType' / 'physicalType' (maps to Adele's authored type vs duckdb type), 'examples', 'quality', and an object-level 'dataGranularityDescription' (free text, same idea as Adele's grain). No unit of measure for columns (verified absent on the schema page) and no temporal coverage. Much of the standard (pricing, roles, team) is irrelevant for a dozen public datasets, so borrowing the SLA block inside 'adele:' is better than switching standard.

projects.name: datacontract-cli
projects.what: Open-source CLI and Python library that lints ODCS contracts and tests real data against them (schema and quality), with import/export to 25+ formats.
projects.overlap: Detection of schema drift and breaking changes, freshness and row count checks, tests run on local Parquet through DuckDB.

The README also points to 'Data Contract Skills' for coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Copilot) and llms.txt files: direct prior art for Adele's SKILL.md, worth reading.

projects.name: dbt sources / model contracts (schema.yml)
projects.what: dbt's YAML properties for sources and models, including declarative freshness thresholds checked by 'dbt freshness'.
projects.overlap: Freshness SLA and status (fresh / warn / error), the column that holds the load time.
projects.takeaways: Verified: 'freshness' has 'warn_after' and 'error_after', each {count, period} with period in minute/hour/day; 'loaded_at_field' or 'loaded_at_query' (dbt v1.10+) says how to compute the latest load time; 'filter' limits the scan. The two-threshold design maps well to Adele's dataset status and email alert: one threshold for 'late' and one for 'failed', with 'loaded_at_field' = fetched_at for append-only datasets or max(delivery_start) for coverage. dbt has no unit field for columns (units go in free 'meta'; this was not verified on a page) and no temporal coverage. Adopting dbt itself is not justified for Adele (fetch and normalize, no SQL transformation graph).

projects.name: DuckLake
projects.what: Lakehouse format from the DuckDB team: metadata in a SQL catalog database, data in Parquet files, with snapshots and time travel.
projects.overlap: Knowledge-time axis (as_of queries), tracking of schema versions, partitioned Parquet, DuckDB engine. An alternative to hand-built append-only + fetched_at.
projects.takeaways: Verified: spec version 1.1 labelled stable; catalog tables include ducklake_snapshot, ducklake_snapshot_changes, ducklake_schema_versions, ducklake_column, ducklake_column_tag, ducklake_tag, ducklake_table_stats, ducklake_table_column_stats, ducklake_file_column_stats, ducklake_partition_info. Time travel syntax verified: 'SELECT * FROM tbl AT (VERSION => 3)' and 'AT (TIMESTAMP => now() - INTERVAL '1 week')'. This gives 'as_of=<timestamp>' for every dataset, including the ones with an overwrite policy, and a record of each schema change. Limits for Adele: snapshot time is the time of Adele's write, which equals knowledge time only if fetches are never backfilled; and 'adele pull' (plain sync of Parquet partitions to a laptop) becomes harder because the files are meaningful only with the catalog. It holds no units, grain or coverage, so it does not replace the descriptor. Worth a deliberate yes/no decision in the spec.
projects.status: Spec 1.1 stable per docs. License not stated on the pages fetched (not verified). Column details of the catalog tables not verified.

projects.name: Croissant (MLCommons) + mlcroissant
projects.what: JSON-LD metadata format for ML datasets built on schema.org/Dataset, with FileObject/FileSet, RecordSet and Field layers. mlcroissant is the Python library.
projects.overlap: Machine-readable description of files, record sets, keys, example records. Discovery by dataset search engines.
projects.takeaways: Verified in spec 1.0 and 1.1: RecordSet has 'key' (fields that uniquely identify a record) and 'examples' (sample records, same idea as Adele's 5 sample rows); Field has 'dataType', 'equivalentProperty', 'annotation'; dataset has 'isLiveDataset' (Boolean), 'version', 'dateModified'. NOT defined: unit of measure on fields, temporalCoverage (can be borrowed from schema.org but the spec does not discuss it), update frequency, freshness, value constraints. For live datasets the spec only says to set isLiveDataset and to omit sha256. So Croissant is weaker than Frictionless + adele block for Adele's needs, and JSON-LD costs more tokens for an agent. Only value: an optional export if the datasets are ever published on Hugging Face or Kaggle. 1.1 adds provenance (PROV-O), usage policies (ODRL) and links to domain vocabularies (from the search result, not read in the spec).
projects.status: Spec 1.1 published 2026-01-29 (search result); spec CC BY-ND 4.0, code Apache 2. Repo 921 stars; 'pip install mlcroissant', Python 3.10+. Latest mlcroissant version not verified.

projects.name: schema.org Dataset (and PropertyValue)
projects.what: The schema.org vocabulary for describing datasets in JSON-LD, used by Google Dataset Search; Croissant and DCAT mappings build on it.
projects.overlap: Temporal coverage notation, units of a measured variable.

projects.name: DCAT 3 (W3C)
projects.what: W3C RDF vocabulary for data catalogs, the base of European open data portals (DCAT-AP).
