results.angle_summary: No existing project fits "append-only Parquet + DuckDB on one box" as a whole. TimeDB (ClickHouse), tshistory (PostgreSQL), XTDB (own Arrow engine) and ArcticDB (BSL license, own format) all replace the storage that Adele already chose. Best fit: build it as plain rows (delivery_start, fetched_at, value) in Parquet and compute as_of with a DuckDB filter plus "latest row per key" (QUALIFY row_number / arg_max). Borrow the vocabulary from TimeDB (valid_time, knowledge_time, change_time), the API shape from ALFRED, Energy Quantified and Volue, and the row-hash trick from dlt to avoid storing unchanged refetches. Challenges to the spec: (1) fetched_at is not the source's publication time. Keep both when the source gives one (ENTSO-E UpdateTime), and declare which one as_of uses. (2) Table-format time travel (DuckLake, Iceberg) versions the table, not the knowledge time, and it ends when snapshots expire. It cannot replace the fetched_at column. (3) DuckLake 1.x is a credible optional layer for atomic commits and schema-drift history.

projects.name: rebase-energy/timedb
projects.what: Open-source Python client for "3-dimensional" time series from the energy sector (Rebase Energy). Stores forecast revisions and corrections as plain rows, with as-of reads.
projects.overlap: Time model: delivery time vs knowledge time, append-only revisions, as_of queries, day-ahead cutoff reads.
projects.takeaways: Verified on README and PyPI: three time columns. valid_time (when the value applies), knowledge_time (when it was predicted or known), change_time (when the row was written or corrected), plus changed_by and annotation. Default read returns the latest value per valid_time; include_knowledge_time=True returns one row per (knowledge_time, valid_time). read_relative() gives per-window day-ahead cutoffs ("what was known at D-1 12:00 for each day"), which is the query that backtests need and that a single as_of timestamp does not cover. Storage is ClickHouse (tables series_values and run_series), so it cannot be reused on Parquet + DuckDB. A search result claimed that Parquet is on its roadmap; the PyPI page does not mention it (not verified). Idea for Adele: adopt the names valid/knowledge/change, and separate "source published at" from "we fetched at".
projects.status: Apache-2.0. PyPI version 0.12.0 released 2026-08-28. 113 stars, 223 commits, no GitHub releases. Active.

projects.name: DuckDB native pattern (append-only rows + ASOF JOIN / QUALIFY)
projects.what: Not a project: the pattern of storing every revision as a row with a knowledge timestamp in Parquet, and computing the as-of view in SQL with DuckDB (filter fetched_at <= T, keep the latest row per key; or ASOF JOIN for per-row cutoffs).
projects.overlap: The whole revisions policy of the spec: append-only with fetched_at and as_of=<timestamp> on Parquet partitions.
projects.takeaways: This is the best fit, because it needs no extra component and `adele pull` keeps working (partitions stay plain Parquet). DuckDB documents ASOF JOIN (match each row to the most recent row at or before its timestamp); the 2025 planning post (https://duckdb.org/2025/02/19/asof-plans.html) notes that probe rows need a unique id when lookup times repeat. Design notes (my recommendation, not from a page): expose per dataset a view or macro `<ds>_asof(ts)` = rows with fetched_at <= ts, QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY grain key ORDER BY fetched_at DESC) = 1, and a `<ds>_latest` view, so that an agent never writes the dedup itself. Append a row only when the value changed (row hash), otherwise a 15-minute refetch multiplies the data. Deletions at the source need a tombstone row. Monthly partitions by delivery time become append-mostly files: late revisions add small files to old months, so plan a compaction step and make `pull` detect changed partitions (file hash or manifest).
projects.status: DuckDB core feature, MIT, active. The exact QUALIFY pattern was not found written up as a reference page (search returned nothing specific).

projects.name: DuckLake (time travel + data change feed)
projects.what: Lakehouse format from the DuckDB team: Parquet data files plus a SQL catalog database (a DuckDB file in the simplest setup) that holds snapshots, schema versions and statistics.
projects.overlap: Server storage layer, schema drift history, incremental sync (change feed), and a second form of as-of (system time of the table).
projects.takeaways: Verified: `SELECT * FROM tbl AT (VERSION => 3)` and `AT (TIMESTAMP => ...)`, attach a whole database at SNAPSHOT_VERSION / SNAPSHOT_TIME, snapshots are kept until explicitly expired. `table_changes('tbl', start, end)` returns inserts, deletes and update pre/post images between two snapshots with snapshot_id and change_type; compaction that expires snapshots limits this feed. Data is Parquet in a `.files` folder and DuckDB can read the files directly, but updates are delete files + new files, so raw files do not equal the current table state (my inference, also flagged by the fetch). Consequences for Adele: (1) DuckLake time travel answers "what did our table contain at T", which equals knowledge time only if every fetch is one commit and snapshots are never expired. Do not use it as the as_of mechanism; keep fetched_at as a column. (2) It is useful for atomic publishing of a fetch, schema evolution history and the change feed for `pull`. (3) It conflicts with "client syncs plain parquet partitions" unless the client also uses DuckLake or the server exports. Catalog options other than a DuckDB file, partitioning and concurrency were not covered on the pages that I read (not checked).
projects.status: Docs show DuckLake 1.1 as stable. A secondary source says v1.0 shipped 2026-04-13 with a backward compatibility guarantee (not verified on a primary page). License not checked (MIT from memory).

projects.name: ALFRED / FRED API real-time periods (St. Louis Fed)
projects.what: The reference public API for vintage (revised) economic series: every observation carries a real-time period during which that value was the published one.
projects.overlap: API and CLI semantics for as_of, revision policy vocabulary, catalog fields describing revisions.
projects.takeaways: Verified: each observation has realtime_start, realtime_end, date, value. Defaults are today ("FRED mode" = what is known now); setting an earlier period gives "ALFRED mode". Open end is the sentinel 9999-12-31; intervals are closed on both ends (Adele uses half-open, which is cleaner). `vintage_dates` accepts any date, not only revision dates. output_type gives four views (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/docs/api/fred/series_observations.html): 1 by real-time period, 2 all observations per vintage, 3 new and revised only, 4 initial release only. Ideas for Adele: offer the same named views per append-only dataset: latest (default), as_of=T, first_release, all_revisions. "first_release" is a frequent need in forecasting evaluation and is cheap with fetched_at. Storing [known_from, known_to) intervals instead of only fetched_at makes as_of a simple range filter, but it requires rewriting the old row (not append-only). Keep fetched_at only and derive known_to in a view.
projects.status: Official public API, active. Pages verified 2026-11.

projects.name: Energy Quantified Python client (instances)
projects.what: Commercial European power and gas data vendor. Its client docs define a clean data model for forecast vintages: a curve of type INSTANCE holds one series per (issued, tag).
projects.overlap: Catalog vocabulary (curve types, resolution, timezone), and the forecast case of knowledge time (issue time, model tag).
projects.takeaways: Verified: curve_type values TIMESERIES, SCENARIO_TIMESERIES, INSTANCE, PERIODS, PERIOD_INSTANCES, OHLC, TRADES, PPA. An instance is identified by issue date (mandatory) + tag (optional, e.g. 'ec' for ECMWF). Resolution = frequency (ISO 8601 durations P1D, PT1H, PT15M, ...) + timezone. Operations: instances.list() (list without loading), latest, and a "relative" forecast query with days_ahead (0 = intraday, 1 = day-ahead) and a filter on the time of day of issue (https://energyquantified-python.readthedocs.io/en/stable/userguide/instances.html). Ideas for Adele: (1) forecasts have an issue time given by the source, which differs from fetched_at. The spec's single knowledge axis should say per dataset whether knowledge time = issued_at (from source) or fetched_at (from Adele). (2) Declare a per-dataset "shape" in the adele: block (timeseries / instances / periods), because a forecast dataset has grain (zone, issued_at, delivery_start), not (zone, delivery_start). (3) A days_ahead helper is worth a documented SQL recipe in the skill.
projects.status: Proprietary service; client docs public and maintained (versions v0.1 to v0.14 seen). Client license not checked.

projects.name: Volue Insight (ex Wattsight) curve types
projects.what: Commercial power market data API. Curves are typed by how the knowledge axis is exposed: TIME_SERIES, TAGGED, INSTANCES, TAGGED_INSTANCES, PAIRED_LIST.
projects.overlap: Same as Energy Quantified: catalog typing of datasets, issue_date semantics, interval conventions.
projects.takeaways: Verified: TIME_SERIES = one series (actuals, backcasts, normals); INSTANCES = one series per issue_date (forecasts); TAGGED = one per tag (ensembles); TAGGED_INSTANCES = per (issue_date, tag). Methods per type: get_data; get_instance(issue_date=...), search_instances(issue_date_from, issue_date_to, with_data), get_latest. "End dates are always excluded from the result" (half-open, same as the Adele spec). An agent calling the wrong method for a type gets MethodNotApplicable. Idea for Adele: two independent vendors converged on the same split (single revised series vs one series per issue time). Put this type in `adele describe` output, and make the CLI refuse as_of on overwrite datasets with an explicit error instead of returning current data silently. Metadata on modification time was not covered on the page (not checked).
projects.status: Proprietary service; docs current (library renamed from wapi-python to volue_insight_timeseries). License of client not checked.

projects.name: dlt (dlthub) scd2 merge strategy
projects.what: Open-source Python ingestion library. Its `scd2` merge strategy keeps history of changed rows with validity columns and a row hash.
projects.overlap: Fetchers and normalization on the server; change detection between successive fetches; schema drift handling.
projects.takeaways: Verified: adds _dlt_valid_from / _dlt_valid_to (names configurable; active rows NULL or a high date via active_record_timestamp). Change detection by a hash of all columns (_dlt_id, or your own row_version_column_name). Rows absent from a full extract are retired (valid_to set), not deleted; with incremental extracts, a merge_key on a partition column retires absent rows only within the partitions present in the extract (this matches "refetch the last N delivery days"). boundary_timestamp lets the pipeline set the knowledge timestamp explicitly instead of the load time. Limits: scd2 updates old rows (sets valid_to), so it is not strictly append-only, and the page does not list which destinations support scd2 (duckdb / filesystem parquet support not verified). Reusable ideas even without dlt: row hash to skip unchanged rows, retirement scoped to the refetched window, explicit boundary timestamp.
projects.status: Apache-2.0 from memory (not checked on page), actively maintained. scd2 support for a plain Parquet destination: not verified.

projects.name: AlphaForge PIT store
projects.what: A Python research library (finance) with a point-in-time accessor backed by a "DuckDBParquetStore". The only project found that combines vintages, DuckDB and Parquet.
projects.overlap: Storage schema for append-only revisions on DuckDB + Parquet; snapshot (as-of) reads.
projects.takeaways: Verified schema: series_key, obs_date, asof_utc (vintage = knowledge timestamp), value, release_time_utc (optional, when the source released it), revision_id, source, meta_json, ingested_utc; unique on (series_key, obs_date, asof_utc). API: PITAccessor.open(root), get_snapshot, build_snapshot_tape; snapshot queries require an explicit asof. Useful point for Adele: it keeps three distinct timestamps (vintage, source release time, ingestion time), which supports the challenge that fetched_at alone is too coarse. It is a long (key, value) schema for scalar series, not wide tables, so the code is not reusable for Adele's tabular datasets. SQL of the as-of query, partitioning, license and repo were not on the page.
projects.status: Docs online. License, repo URL, version and activity: not verified. Probably a small project.

projects.name: Timeseries Refinery / tshistory (Pythonian)
projects.what: A versioned time series store on PostgreSQL ("Timeseries store with version control") with a web UI and formula layer (the Refinery). Used in energy and commodity trading.
projects.overlap: Revisions and as-of reads; backtest helpers.
projects.takeaways: From search snippets of PyPI pages (primary pages failed to load): every insert creates a version; `tsa.get(name, revision_date=...)` returns the series as it stood at that time; history() returns versions by insertion date; `staircase` and `block_staircase` (parameters revision_freq, revision_tz) build a series from successive revisions for backtesting, i.e. "value known a fixed delta before delivery". Ideas: the staircase query is the third as-of shape (after fixed as_of and per-day cutoff) and should be a documented recipe. Storage is PostgreSQL with per-series tables and diffs, and the unit is a single scalar series, so it does not match Parquet + DuckDB tabular datasets.
projects.status: Exists on PyPI (versions up to at least 0.14.1 seen in search). License, latest version and date NOT verified: pypi.org pages returned a load error, readthedocs URL 404, sourcehut repo 502.

projects.name: dbt snapshots (SCD type 2)
projects.what: dbt's built-in mechanism to turn a mutable source table into a history table with validity intervals, by comparing the source at each run.
projects.overlap: Revision capture for sources that overwrite in place; hard-delete policy; caveats of polling.
projects.takeaways: Verified: strategies `timestamp` (uses the source's updated_at) and `check` (compares columns, uses run time). Meta columns dbt_valid_from, dbt_valid_to, dbt_scd_id, dbt_updated_at; hard_deletes = ignore | invalidate | new_record (adds dbt_is_deleted). Documented caveat that applies directly to Adele: a snapshot only records the state when it runs, so changes between two runs are lost and the recorded time is the run time, not the time of the change. So Adele's knowledge time has the resolution of the fetch schedule, and the catalog should say so ("knowledge time is accurate to within the refresh interval"). Also: snapshots cannot be rebuilt, so the append-only store needs a backup, unlike the rest that can be refetched. Adopting dbt itself is too heavy for a dozen datasets.
projects.status: dbt Core Apache-2.0 (from memory, not checked), docs current. dbt-duckdb adapter support for snapshots: not checked.

projects.name: Feast point-in-time joins
projects.what: Open-source feature store. Its historical retrieval joins feature rows to an entity dataframe so that each training row only sees values available at its own timestamp.
projects.overlap: Per-row as-of semantics for agents that build training sets from Adele data (leakage avoidance).
projects.takeaways: Verified: for each entity row, Feast scans backward from the entity timestamp up to a TTL on event_timestamp. By default it does NOT exclude backfilled or corrected values that arrived later: created_timestamp is used only to deduplicate. Only `filter_by_created_timestamp=True` enforces created <= entity timestamp, and not all offline stores support it. Lesson for Adele: a one-axis as-of join on delivery time does not prevent leakage; the knowledge axis must be in the filter. This is exactly the error that an agent will make with ASOF JOIN on delivery_start, so the skill should state it and give the two-axis recipe. Feast as software is not relevant (no feature serving in scope). DuckDB offline store: not verified on this page.
projects.status: Apache-2.0 (from memory), active; docs current. Not checked further.

projects.name: XTDB v2
projects.what: A bitemporal SQL database (SQL:2011 valid time + system time on every table), Postgres wire protocol, storage as Arrow files on an object store.
projects.overlap: Full bitemporal model and query syntax.
projects.takeaways: From search results (launch post https://www.xtdb.com/blog/launching-xtdb-v2 and repo https://github.com/xtdb/xtdb): system time and valid time are tracked automatically, columns _valid_from/_valid_to, storage is its own Arrow format (not Parquet), JVM server. It would replace DuckDB and Parquet, add a JVM service, and break `pull`. Take only the vocabulary: SQL:2011 names (valid time, system time) and the rule that every table is temporal by default. A guide exists for streaming XTDB results into DuckDB through ADBC (https://docs.xtdb.com/adbc/guides/streaming-into-duckdb), which confirms that it is a separate engine.
projects.status: MPL-2.0; v2 GA June 2025; v2.1.0 dated 2025-12-01 per a third-party page. Primary pages not fetched: release data not verified.

projects.name: ArcticDB (Man Group)
projects.what: A versioned DataFrame store for Python (every write creates a version; snapshots; read with as_of), on LMDB or S3.
projects.overlap: Versioned reads (as_of by version, snapshot or timestamp).
projects.takeaways: Verified on the licensing page: Business Source License 1.1; a commercial agreement is required for business use, including research and dev environments; each version converts to Apache 2.0 after two years. This alone rules it out for a team tool. Technically it versions whole symbols (dataframes) in its own format, with no SQL and no Parquet, and its "bitemporal" is version time of the write, not a second axis on rows (same limit as table-format time travel).
projects.status: BSL 1.1, actively developed (docs 6.2.x seen). The licensing page fetched may be an older docs version.

projects.name: Iceberg / Delta / lakeFS / Dolt (table or repository versioning)
projects.what: Table formats with snapshot time travel (Iceberg, Delta), and Git-like versioning of object stores (lakeFS) or of a MySQL-compatible database (Dolt).
projects.overlap: System-time versioning of the server's storage; alternative to DuckLake.
projects.takeaways: From search results: the DuckDB iceberg extension reads historical snapshots (snapshot_from_id / snapshot_from_timestamp, or AT on attached catalogs). All four version the container (table snapshot, commit), not the knowledge time of a row, and history ends at snapshot expiry or compaction. On one box with DuckDB, Iceberg and Delta need a catalog and bring multi-engine interoperability that Adele does not need; DuckLake covers the same need with less. lakeFS needs its own server; Dolt has its own storage engine and is not Parquet. None of them removes the need for a fetched_at column. pytemporal (https://pypi.org/project/pytemporal/, MIT/Apache, v1.4.27 of 2025-12-04) is a related in-memory Rust processor that maintains effective/as-of intervals on DataFrames; it rewrites intervals, so it does not fit append-only either.
projects.status: Iceberg time travel in DuckDB seen in search snippets only. Dolt docs redirect not followed, lakeFS not fetched: not verified.

projects.name: dlt (dlthub)
projects.what: Python library (no server, no daemon) that extracts from APIs, files and SQL, infers and versions a schema, and loads to a destination, including a local filesystem destination that writes Parquet.
projects.overlap: Server fetchers, normalization to Parquet, incremental fetch, the rule "never change the schema silently", append-only revisions with a load id.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the docs. (1) Schema contracts: modes evolve / freeze / discard_row / discard_value, set separately for tables, columns and data_type. With freeze, a new column or a type change raises DataValidationError (wrapped in PipelineStepFailed) and nothing is loaded. This is the closest ready-made match to the Adele drift rule. (2) Alerting: only a Slack helper and Sentry are documented. No email, and no automatic schema alert: the docs show how to loop over load_info.load_packages[].schema_update and send the message yourself. So the email is still Adele code. (3) Incremental: dlt.sources.incremental(cursor_path, initial_value, end_value) with half-open ranges by default, backfill with end_value that does not touch the stored state, a lag window for late data. (4) Audit trail: tables _dlt_loads and _dlt_version store a schema_version_hash per load, a good model for the knowledge-time axis. (5) Limit that matters for Adele: the filesystem destination partitions through a path layout with placeholders based on load time (YYYY, MM, load_id), not on a data column, and merge falls back to append for plain Parquet. Partitioning by a column (delivery month) needs table_format=delta with the partition hint, which adds a Delta log and complicates `adele pull`. Practical design: use dlt for extract + contract + state into a staging DuckDB, then let Adele write the month partitions with DuckDB COPY ... PARTITION_BY.
projects.status: Apache 2.0, 6.1k stars, Python 3.10 to 3.14 (seen on README). Active: a dlthub blog post on schema monitoring is dated 2026-04-24, docs mention version 1.26. Exact latest release date not checked.

projects.name: systemd timers (or cron) + plain Python + DuckDB
projects.what: The baseline with no framework: one systemd timer and service unit per dataset, running a Python fetcher that writes Parquet with DuckDB.
projects.overlap: Scheduled fetchers on one linux box, failure alert emails, ETA of next refresh.
projects.takeaways: From the search summary of the Arch wiki and related pages (not read in full): systemd timers have no equivalent of cron MAILTO. The standard pattern is OnFailure=status_email_user@%n.service, a template unit that sends the mail. Known trap: systemd can kill the mail process before it finishes. Persistent=true runs a job that was missed while the machine was off. For Adele: the timer's OnCalendar expression is the source of truth for "ETA of next refresh" (systemctl list-timers gives the next trigger), so the catalog field can be computed from it instead of authored twice. Schema drift check is about 20 lines: compare DuckDB parquet_schema() (or DESCRIBE) of the new batch with the descriptor in git, and refuse to publish on any difference. A Kestra blueprint (https://kestra.io/blueprints/duckdb-parquet-schema-evolution-guard) does exactly this with a full outer join on column name and three labels: DROPPED_COLUMN, DATA_TYPE_MUTATION, NEW_COLUMN. For a dozen sources this baseline is sufficient, and it gives nothing out of the box: retries, run history and emails are all Adele code.
projects.status: Part of every linux distribution. Arch wiki page seen only through search results, not fetched directly.

projects.name: Healthchecks (healthchecks.io, self-hostable)
projects.what: Open-source monitor for cron jobs (Python/Django). Each job pings a URL. The service sends an alert when a ping is late or when the job reports a failure.
projects.overlap: Email alert when a dataset status changes, specifically the case that a failure email cannot cover: the fetcher did not run at all.
projects.takeaways: Verified: BSD-3-Clause, self-hostable (Docker images for amd64 and arm), email alerts through SMTP, a check is defined by Period + Grace Time or by a cron expression. A job signals failure by appending /fail or /<exit-status> to the ping URL (non-zero = failure). Design point for Adele: an email sent by the fetcher on exception misses a dead box, a disabled timer, or a hung process. A check per dataset with the dataset's cron expression and a grace time covers these cases, and "late" becomes a third status next to "fetch failed" and "schema drift". If self-hosting one more service is too much, the hosted service has the same API (free tier not checked). Adele could also implement the same rule itself: status = stale when now > expected_refresh + grace.
projects.status: BSD-3-Clause. Maintenance activity and last release not checked (README release section was empty in the fetch). The /start signal and log attachment exist in my memory but were not confirmed on the fetched page.

projects.name: Dagster
projects.what: Asset-based orchestrator in Python with a web UI, a daemon for schedules and sensors, asset checks and freshness policies.
projects.overlap: Scheduling, freshness and ETA, schema drift detection, failure emails, dataset status.
projects.takeaways: Verified. (1) Freshness policies exist in open source but are a preview that must be enabled in dagster.yaml (freshness: enabled: True). Two kinds: time window ("materialized at least every 24 h") and cron (deadline + lower-bound window). The cron form is a good model for the Adele "refresh" block: expected schedule + allowed delay --> status fresh/stale. (2) build_column_schema_change_checks(assets=[...]) is built in: it compares the column schema of each materialization with the previous one and flags added columns, removed columns and changed types (seen in a search summary of the table-metadata docs page, page itself not fetched because of a redirect). (3) Email: make_email_on_run_failure_sensor sends mail by SMTP on a failed job. The docs example for checks uses a separate check job + this sensor. Direct alerts on a failed asset check or on a freshness violation are listed under Dagster+ (paid). So in open source, Dagster gives drift detection + failure email with some wiring, the most complete of the orchestrators reviewed. Cost: webserver + daemon as two services, and Postgres recommended over SQLite for production (third-party guide, not verified in official docs). Heavy for 12 fetchers, but it is the tool to choose if a UI with run history is wanted.
projects.status: Apache 2.0 (from memory, not re-checked). Actively developed in 2026 (docs current). Freshness policies marked preview, API may change.

projects.name: PUDL (Catalyst Cooperative)
projects.what: Open-source pipeline that turns US public energy data (EIA, FERC, EPA: spreadsheets, CSV, database dumps) into Parquet tables plus a DuckDB database, rebuilt every night.
projects.overlap: The closest whole-system analogue: public energy sources of mixed formats --> Parquet + DuckDB + JSON metadata, daily refresh, published for programmatic use.
projects.takeaways: Verified on README: outputs are Parquet files with metadata stored as JSON next to them, packaged also as a DuckDB database. SQLite output is deprecated and stops in 2027 (a sign that Parquet + DuckDB is the right target). Nightly builds are published (AWS Open Data Registry), with periodic archived versions. The repo has a dbt directory. From search results: the code has a module pudl.dagster.asset_checks (docs for v2026.6.1), so it uses Dagster with asset checks. Not verified in this session: whether the metadata is still a Frictionless datapackage (it was, from memory) and the use of Pandera. Worth reading for Adele: how they author table and field metadata (units, descriptions) once in code and generate descriptors and docs from it, and how they version nightly vs stable outputs.
projects.status: MIT (code), CC-BY-4.0 (data). Active: docs versions v2026.1.0 and v2026.6.1 seen in search results.

projects.name: Kestra
projects.what: Declarative orchestrator (flows in YAML) on the JVM, with a UI and a large plugin catalog.
projects.overlap: Scheduling, failure emails for all flows with one rule, a ready blueprint for Parquet schema drift.
projects.takeaways: Verified. Runs from one executable JAR, needs Java 21+. `server local` uses an H2 file database (no external DB). `server standalone` needs a configured database. Can run as a systemd service. Failure email for everything in one place: the blueprint https://kestra.io/blueprints/failure-alert-email is a flow in the system namespace with a Flow trigger on states FAILED and WARNING and a task io.kestra.plugin.email.MailSend over SMTP. The page does not mark it Enterprise. Schema drift blueprint (see baseline entry) uses DuckDB parquet_schema() against a baseline file and alerts on Slack. So Kestra gives "email on any failure" with about 15 lines of YAML, and drift detection as a copyable pattern, not a built-in. Costs for Adele: a JVM service next to a Python code base, fetch logic split between YAML and scripts. Note from search: Kestra removed its Singer plugin in 1.0.
projects.status: Apache 2.0 for the open-source edition (from memory, not re-checked). Active in 2026 (v1.x docs). Whether the email plugin ships in the default open-source image was not confirmed (the JAR ships without plugins, they are installed separately).

projects.name: Prefect (v3, self-hosted server)
projects.what: Python orchestrator: decorated flows and tasks, a server with UI, deployments with cron schedules, automations that react to events.
projects.overlap: Scheduling, retries, failure notification.
projects.takeaways: Partly verified. Search results agree that the dedicated "send email" automation action is only in Prefect Cloud. On a self-hosted server the options are: the prefect-email package (EmailServerCredentials block + email_send_message called from a flow or a failure hook), or an automation that calls a webhook. One third-party source claims PREFECT_SERVER_SMTP_* settings enable email on self-hosted servers. I could not confirm it in official docs. No schema drift feature. Lighter than Dagster to adopt for existing Python functions, but it has no notion of dataset or freshness, so the Adele catalog status would still be computed by Adele.
projects.status: Apache 2.0 (from memory). Active (3.4.x seen in community threads). The official alerts tutorial URL returned 404 after redirect, so the Cloud-only email claim rests on search summaries.

projects.name: Git scraping + git-history (Simon Willison)
projects.what: Pattern: a scheduled job fetches a resource, writes it to a file in a git repo and commits only when it changed. git-history then converts the commit history of that file into SQLite tables.
projects.overlap: Knowledge-time axis and revision policy (append-only with fetched_at, as_of queries), change detection.
projects.takeaways: Verified. The original example runs on GitHub Actions cron every 20 minutes at offset minutes (6, 26, 46) to avoid the top of the hour: a detail worth copying for the 15-minute fetchers. git-history (https://github.com/simonw/git-history, Apache-2.0) with --id builds tables item (latest version of each record), item_version (one row per captured version, by default only the changed columns), item_changed and commits. This is a concrete bitemporal schema: commit time = knowledge time. For Adele the storage does not fit (git is poor with Parquet and with 15-minute data over years), but two ideas transfer: (1) store a revision only when the content hash of the row changed, so append-only tables stay small. (2) Keep the raw fetched file, with its fetch timestamp, before normalization, so that a parser bug can be replayed. The authored yaml descriptors in git already give the same audit trail for the schema.
projects.status: Blog post from 2020, pattern still in wide use. git-history: Apache-2.0, last release not checked (it was quiet for years, from memory).

projects.name: Bruin + ingestr
projects.what: Bruin is a CLI that combines ingestion, SQL/Python transformations and data quality checks in one project. ingestr is its single-command tool that copies data from a source to a destination.
projects.overlap: Ingestion, quality checks, DuckDB and local Parquet as destinations.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the READMEs. Bruin: Apache-2.0, built-in quality checks, runs on a local machine, EC2 or GitHub Actions. The README mentions no scheduler and no notifications, so on one box it still needs cron, and the email is still custom. ingestr (https://github.com/bruin-data/ingestr): strategies append, merge, delete+insert. DuckDB as source and destination, local Parquet file as destination. License is NOT plain open source: Functional Source License 1.1, each version becomes Apache 2.0 after two years (internal use is allowed). ingestr targets database and SaaS sources. ENTSO-E style REST/XML and xlsx files would still need custom Python. Idea to keep: the Bruin asset file, where a SQL or Python file carries its metadata and its column checks in a header block, is close to the Adele yaml descriptor + fetcher pair.

projects.what: The standard DAG scheduler in Python.
projects.overlap: Scheduling, retries, failure email.

The only reason to choose it would be existing team knowledge. dlt has an option allow_external_schedulers that takes the time interval from Airflow instead of its own state (verified on the dlt cursor page).

results.angle_summary:
No open-source tool gives "email on schema drift" out of the box. Closest: dlt schema contracts (freeze --> exception, nothing loaded) and Dagster build_column_schema_change_checks plus its SMTP run-failure sensor. Dagster's direct alerts on checks and freshness are paid (Dagster+). dlt documents only Slack and Sentry. Kestra gives email on any failure with one system flow.

Recommendation: systemd timers + plain Python, dlt as a library for extraction, incremental state and contract, and a dead man's switch (Healthchecks or an equivalent rule in Adele). An orchestrator is not justified for 12 sources, unless a UI with run history is wanted (then Dagster).

Challenges to the spec: (1) dlt's Parquet filesystem destination partitions by load time, not by a data column, so Adele must write the delivery-month partitions itself (DuckDB COPY PARTITION_BY). (2) Add a third status "stale / fetcher did not run": a failure email cannot report a job that never started. (3) Derive the refresh ETA from the timer definition.

No listed tool covers Adele's whole need, and most are too heavy or tied to dbt. The checks themselves are small: (1) compare DuckDB `parquet_schema()`/DESCRIBE with the types in the descriptor, (2) compare now with max(fetched_at) and max(delivery_start), (3) email when the status changes. Recommendation: write these in about 200 lines of DuckDB SQL and Python, and reuse two components: frictionless-py (validate the descriptor and the raw csv/xlsx at ingest) and a dead man's switch outside the box (Healthchecks), because the box cannot email about its own death. Challenges to the spec: (a) define freshness on both time axes with warn and error thresholds, plus a cron deadline with a tolerance window (Dagster model) to compute the ETA; (b) classify schema changes (added column, dropped column, type change) and define which ones block publication; (c) ODCS + datacontract-cli is the main competitor to Frictionless as the descriptor format: decide explicitly.

projects.name: frictionless-py (Frictionless Framework)
projects.what: Python library and CLI to describe, extract, validate and transform tabular data against Frictionless Table Schema / Data Package descriptors.
projects.overlap: Catalog descriptor format (Adele already uses Data Package) and schema validation of raw sources at ingest (csv, xlsx, sql, parquet).
projects.takeaways: Verified: the baseline check (always on) reports incorrect-label, missing-label, extra-label, type-error, constraint-error, primary-key, unique-error, foreign-key (https://framework.frictionlessdata.io/docs/checks/baseline.html). These error codes map directly to a classification of schema drift (missing-label = dropped column, extra-label = new column, type-error = type change). PyPI extras include `parquet` (pyarrow>=14) and `duckdb` (duckdb>=0.8, duckdb-engine, sqlalchemy<=2.0.35: this pin on SQLAlchemy can conflict with other packages). Use it for two things: validate the authored yaml descriptors in CI, and validate each fetched raw file before normalization. It validates row by row in Python, so for the normalized Parquet partitions a DuckDB query is faster. It has no freshness check and no alerting.
projects.status: MIT. Active: PyPI shows 5.21.0 released 2026-10-15 and 5.20.0 on 2026-10-08 (verified on pypi.org). 235 open issues, 50 open PRs on GitHub.

projects.name: Healthchecks (healthchecks.io, self-hostable)
projects.what: Dead man's switch for cron jobs: each job pings an URL, and the service alerts when a ping does not arrive on time or when the job signals a failure.
projects.overlap: Alerting on fetch failure, and detection of a fetcher or a whole server that stopped silently (the case that Adele's own email alert cannot cover).
projects.takeaways: Verified: each check has a Period and a Grace Time, or a cron expression; the job signals failure with `<ping-url>/fail` or `<ping-url>/<exit status>` (non-zero = failure) (https://healthchecks.io/docs/signaling_failures/). 25+ notification integrations and email. Design ideas for Adele: one check per dataset with the same cron as the fetcher; alerts are sent on a change of state (up --> down, down --> up), which is exactly "email when a dataset status changes". Use the hosted service or a second machine: a dead man's switch on the same box dies with the box. Self-hosting needs Python 3.12+, Django 6.1, a database (PostgreSQL/MySQL/MariaDB; SQLite in the development setup), SMTP, and a `sendalerts` process that runs constantly: more than Adele needs on one box, so the hosted free tier is the simpler option (free tier limits not checked).
projects.status: BSD-3-Clause. Active (README requires Django 6.1). Latest release number not seen on the page.

projects.name: Data Contract CLI (datacontract-cli) + Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS)
projects.what: CLI and Python library that lints a YAML data contract (ODCS), tests real data against it, and compares two versions of a contract. ODCS (https://github.com/bitol-io/open-data-contract-standard, v3.2.0, Apache-2.0, LF AI & Data) is the contract format.
projects.overlap: Catalog descriptor (alternative to Frictionless), schema validation of local Parquet with DuckDB, freshness check, detection of breaking schema changes.
projects.takeaways: Verified: servers of `type: local` with `format: parquet|csv|json|xlsx|delta|xml` and a glob `path` (https://cli.datacontract.com/testing/local); DuckDB is an optional extra (`duckdb>=1.5,<1.6`) and appears to be the engine for local files (not stated outright). `datacontract test` exits with code 1 on failure. Only two service levels become executable checks: freshness (now - MAX(timestamp column) < value) and retention (uses MIN); latency, frequency and timeOfAvailability are documentation only (https://cli.datacontract.com/service-levels). `datacontract changelog` diffs two contract versions and `datacontract breaking` fails on a breaking change: copy this idea for Adele (diff the authored descriptor against the observed DuckDB types, classify as breaking or not). ODCS slaProperties (latency, frequency, retention, with value/unit/element) is a ready vocabulary for Adele's `adele:` block. Core dependencies are heavy for one box (boto3, sqlglot, Jinja2, pydantic, about 20 packages). It has no notion of units per field (not found on the ODCS README) and no bitemporal concept. Soda is not a dependency (only a SodaCL export).
projects.status: MIT. PyPI latest 1.2.9 (release date not seen, the page did not load). Python >=3.10,<3.15.

projects.name: DuckDB parquet_schema() diff pattern (Kestra blueprint as a written example)
projects.what: Not a library: a pattern that reads the footers of two Parquet files with DuckDB's `parquet_schema()`, joins them with a FULL OUTER JOIN on column name, and reports the differences.
projects.overlap: Detection of schema drift on the normalized Parquet partitions, with the engine that Adele already has.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the page: statuses DROPPED_COLUMN, DATA_TYPE_MUTATION, NEW_COLUMN (the last one only fails when `fail_on_new_columns` is true), and only footers are read so the cost does not depend on the size of the data. For Adele: the baseline should be the descriptor in git (duckdb types), not a previous file; run the diff on the freshly written partition before it is published, and set the dataset status to `schema_drift` instead of publishing. Weakness of the blueprint to avoid: its alert only describes the first changed column. This is the approach with zero new dependencies and is my recommended core.
projects.status: Blueprint page verified. No license or maintenance question (it is 20 lines of SQL).

projects.name: dbt source freshness / dbt freshness
projects.what: dbt's declarative freshness check: per source table, a timestamp column and two thresholds, evaluated by one SQL query.
projects.overlap: Freshness model and its vocabulary in the catalog (`adele:` block).
projects.takeaways: Verified: config is `warn_after: {count, period}` and `error_after: {count, period}` (period = minute|hour|day), `loaded_at_field` or `loaded_at_query` (dbt 1.10+), and a `filter` to limit the scan; the query is `select max(loaded_at_field), current_timestamp`. Without `loaded_at_field`, dbt falls back to warehouse metadata (last modified time). The docs now call `dbt source freshness` a legacy command and recommend `dbt freshness`; results go to `sources.json`. Ideas for Adele: two thresholds (warn, error) instead of one; three states (fresh, stale-warn, stale-error); a machine-readable result file per run. Adele has two candidates for `loaded_at_field` (fetched_at = knowledge time, max(delivery_start) = delivery time) and should report both, because a fetch can succeed while the source publishes no new rows. Adopting dbt itself would add a large tool for a system with no SQL transformations.
projects.status: Docs page verified 2026-11. dbt-core license and version not checked.

projects.name: Dagster freshness policies
projects.what: Freshness policies attached to assets in the Dagster orchestrator: a time window or a cron deadline.
projects.overlap: Freshness and "ETA of next refresh" semantics.
projects.takeaways: Verified: two policy types. Time window: `fail_window` and an optional shorter `warn_window` (both >= 60 s). Cron: `deadline_cron` + `lower_bound_delta` (the window before each deadline in which the refresh must happen) + `timezone` (default UTC). The cron model fits Adele better than a plain maximum age: a daily dataset published at 13:00 is "fresh" if a successful fetch happened in [deadline - delta, deadline], and the next deadline tick is the ETA to show in `adele describe`. API churn is a warning: the original FreshnessPolicy is deprecated since 1.6, freshness checks are superseded since 1.12. Alerts are documented under Dagster+ (the paid product); the page shows no alerting for OSS. Dagster as a whole (daemon, web server, database) is too large for a dozen cron fetchers.
projects.status: Docs page verified 2026-11. License and latest version not checked.

projects.name: Soda Core v4
projects.what: Engine that verifies YAML data contracts (schema and data quality checks) against a data source, through a CLI (`soda contract verify`) and a Python API.
projects.overlap: Schema validation, freshness check, DuckDB as data source.
projects.takeaways: Verified: a `soda-duckdb` package exists (depends on duckdb>=1.2,<2). The contract language has a `schema` check with `allow_extra_columns` and `allow_other_column_order`, and a `freshness` check with `column` and `threshold: {unit: hour, must_be_less_than: 24}` (https://docs.soda.io/reference/contract-language-reference). The two flags are a good idea for Adele's policy on drift (is a new column an error, is a new column order an error). Blocking point: the repo LICENSE is Elastic License 2.0 and PyPI labels soda-duckdb as "Proprietary"; ELv2 forbids offering the software as a hosted service and mentions license key functionality. Soda Cloud is not required for local verification, but anomaly detection needs it. Not worth the license question for checks that are a few SQL lines.
projects.status: Elastic License 2.0 (verified in the LICENSE file), not open source. Very active: soda-duckdb 4.30.0 uploaded 2026-11-05. v3 (soda-core-*) is the legacy line, pinned at 3.5.x.

projects.name: Pandera
projects.what: Python library that validates dataframes (pandas, polars, pyspark, ibis and others) against a schema declared in code.
projects.overlap: Schema and value validation in the fetchers, before writing Parquet.
projects.takeaways: Verified: PyPI extras include polars, ibis, pyarrow, narwhals, io and frictionless. `pandera.io.pandas_io.from_frictionless_schema()` builds a DataFrameSchema from a Frictionless schema (path, dict or object): names, types, constraints (minimum/maximum --> in_range, maxLength, pattern) and primary keys (non-nullable and unique) are mapped; foreign keys and formats are not; documented for pandas only. So Adele's descriptor could stay the single source of truth and pandera could enforce it inside a fetcher. Use it only if the fetchers use pandas/polars dataframes and need value checks (ranges, allowed zones). It works on dataframes in memory, has no freshness check, no alerting, and no DuckDB-native path except through ibis (not checked in detail). Optional: frictionless-py alone covers the same descriptor.
projects.status: MIT. Very active: 0.36.0 released 2026-11-10 (verified on pypi.org).

projects.name: Pointblank (Posit)
projects.what: Python data validation library with validation plans, thresholds, HTML reports, a CLI and YAML plans.
projects.overlap: Validation of Parquet/DuckDB tables with thresholds and notifications; agent-facing features.
projects.takeaways: Verified in the README: backends are Polars, Pandas, PySpark, and databases through Ibis (DuckDB listed), plus CSV and Parquet files. Plans can be written in YAML (`pb.yaml_interrogate`), the `pb` CLI has `validate`/`run`/`scan` with `--exit-code`. Three threshold levels (warning, error, critical) with Actions and FinalActions (a Slack notification helper is shown; email not seen). It has features for LLMs: `DraftValidation` sends a summary of the table (column types, statistics, sample values) to an LLM, and there is an MCP server. That table summary is close to what `adele describe` should return, so it is worth reading. Freshness and a whole-schema check were not mentioned in the README (not verified beyond it). Not listed in the task.
projects.status: MIT. Latest version and release date not seen on the page (not checked).

projects.name: dlt schema contracts (dlthub)
projects.what: The Python ingestion library dlt lets each pipeline declare what happens when incoming data does not fit the stored schema.
projects.overlap: The rule "never changes schema silently" in the fetchers; possibly the whole fetch-and-normalize layer.
projects.takeaways: Verified: four modes (evolve, freeze, discard_row, discard_value) applied separately to three entities (tables, columns, data_type). `freeze` raises DataValidationError (wrapped in PipelineStepFailed) and loads nothing; the exception carries the table, the column, the violated entity and the offending item. Idea for Adele: a policy per dataset of the same shape, for example `columns: freeze, data_type: freeze`, and reuse the content of that exception as the body of the alert email. The page describes no notification mechanism other than the exception. dlt could also replace Adele's fetchers and Parquet writer (it has filesystem/Parquet and DuckDB destinations from memory: not verified on this page), but it manages its own schema and state, which would compete with the Frictionless descriptor as source of truth.

projects.name: Great Expectations (GX Core)
projects.what: Python data quality framework built on "Expectations" (unit tests for data), with validation results and generated documentation.
projects.overlap: Schema and value validation.
projects.takeaways: Verified on PyPI: 18 core dependencies including pandas, numpy, scipy, altair, marshmallow and cryptography, so it is heavy for one box. The README does not mention DuckDB, Parquet or freshness (it points to a compatibility reference that I did not open). It needs its own context, data sources, suites and checkpoints, which duplicates Adele's descriptor. Only idea worth taking: the naming of expectations (`expect_column_values_to_be_between` etc.) is a known vocabulary that agents recognize.

projects.name: Elementary (elementary-data)
projects.what: Open-source CLI and dbt package for data observability on top of dbt: anomaly tests, schema change tests, a report, alerts.
projects.overlap: Schema drift detection, freshness anomalies, alerting.

The `schema_changes` test alerts on a deleted table, deleted or added columns, and a change of a column's data type (https://docs.elementary-data.com/data-tests/schema-tests/schema-changes): the same three classes as the DuckDB diff pattern. OSS alert channels are Slack and Microsoft Teams; email was not mentioned. The CLI pulls boto3, google-cloud-storage, azure-storage-blob and posthog (telemetry). Too much for Adele, which has no dbt.

projects.what: Young Python data quality library built on DuckDB, with schema tracking, freshness monitoring, data contracts and notifiers.

But adoption is almost zero (4 stars, 1 fork, 59 commits) and the README makes marketing claims ("10x faster") that I could not check. Do not depend on it; read its schema snapshot and diff code as an example of the design. Not listed in the task.

It requires dbt and supports Postgres, BigQuery, Snowflake and Redshift only (no DuckDB). Drop it from the list. With a dozen datasets that have known publication schedules, explicit thresholds are simpler and easier to explain.

results.angle_summary: No single project gives authenticated remote SQL plus incremental pull. The least custom code is two stock parts. (1) Static Parquet partitions behind Caddy/nginx with a bearer check per API key: DuckDB httpfs reads them with range requests and an HTTP secret, and pull is a manifest diff (about 100 lines) or rclone. (2) Quack (DuckDB 2.0 core extension) for server-side SQL: per-user tokens through a SQL macro, database attached read-only, reverse proxy for TLS. It can replace a custom HTTP query API, but only DuckDB clients connect. Challenges to the spec: DuckLake snapshots (AT TIMESTAMP, table_changes) already implement knowledge time and as_of, and its file list is a ready pull manifest, so consider it instead of hand-made month partitions plus fetched_at. Plain HTTP has no documented glob, so descriptors must list partition files. GizmoSQL is in maintenance, Seafowl and ROAPI lack read auth, Delta Sharing and Iceberg REST need object storage.

projects.name: DuckDB httpfs + static file server (nginx/Caddy) with HTTP bearer secret
projects.what: DuckDB's core httpfs extension reads remote Parquet over HTTP(S) with range requests, so that only the footer and the needed columns are downloaded. Any static web server that honours Range headers can be the data server.
projects.overlap: Remote query without a server-side query engine, API key per team member, and the transport for `adele pull`.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the page: `CREATE SECRET http_auth (TYPE http, BEARER_TOKEN 'token');` or `EXTRA_HTTP_HEADERS MAP {'Authorization': 'Bearer token'}`; `read_parquet([...])` over a list of URLs is supported; partial reads use the Parquet metadata plus range requests; a DuckDB database file can also be attached read-only over HTTPS. The page says nothing about glob or hive partitioning over plain HTTP, so Adele should publish an explicit list of partition files per dataset (in the descriptor or a manifest.json) and the client should build the `read_parquet([...])` list from it. Secrets accept a SCOPE (seen in a DuckDB test file), so the key is sent only to the Adele host. The key check itself is a few lines of reverse proxy config (not verified here: nginx auth_request or a Caddy matcher on the Authorization header). With this design `adele query` can run in the local DuckDB against remote files, and the server needs no query API at all for the Python/CLI client.
projects.status: Core DuckDB extension, MIT, actively maintained; docs exist for DuckDB 2.0 (verified). Behaviour of the HTTP secret on a list of partitioned files and behind nginx was not tested.

projects.name: Quack (DuckDB client-server protocol)
projects.what: Official DuckDB extension that turns a DuckDB instance into an HTTP server to which other DuckDB instances attach (`ATTACH 'quack:host' AS remote`). Announced 2026-05-12, autoloadable core extension since DuckDB 1.5.3.
projects.overlap: Server-side `adele query "<duckdb sql>"` with authentication, in place of a custom HTTP SQL API.
projects.takeaways: Verified: server starts with `CALL quack_serve('quack:localhost', token = '...')`; client uses `CREATE SECRET (TYPE quack, TOKEN '...', SCOPE 'quack:host')` then ATTACH, or `quack_query`. Security page: `quack_authentication_function` can be a SQL MACRO that looks the token up in a `quack_tokens` table, so one token per team member is an INSERT/DELETE. `quack_authorization_function` exists, but the docs say that the regex example is not a robust read-only filter and recommend to attach the database read-only. Docs advise not to expose Quack directly: bind to localhost and put nginx or Caddy in front (recipes provided). The EXTRA_HTTP_HEADERS option of the secret passes headers to a proxy. Limits: only DuckDB clients with the extension (fine for a Python lib that embeds DuckDB, not for curl); ATTACH binds every remote table and fails if one fails. Pull could be `COPY ... TO` from the attached remote, but that copies rows, not partition files, so a file-level sync is still better for `pull`. A definite.app blog post shows Quack used as the DuckLake catalog (seen in search results, not read).
projects.status: MIT. The GitHub README (https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-quack) still says pre-release and experimental; the 2.0 docs carry no maturity label. No release date found on the repo page.

projects.name: DuckLake (v1.0) and Frozen DuckLake over HTTPS
projects.what: Lakehouse format from DuckDB Labs: Parquet data files plus a SQL catalog database (DuckDB, SQLite or PostgreSQL) holding snapshots, schemas and file lists. v1.0 released 2026-04-13; v1.1 was announced for September 2026.
projects.overlap: Catalog and storage layout, knowledge-time axis (as_of queries), detection of schema changes, the manifest for incremental pull, read-only serving over HTTPS.
projects.takeaways: Verified: a read-only lake is served from any HTTPS endpoint: `ATTACH 'https://.../x.ducklake' AS x (TYPE ducklake);`. A frozen lake is updated by replacing the catalog file. Time travel: `SELECT * FROM tbl AT (TIMESTAMP => ...)`, `AT (VERSION => 3)`, `ATTACH ... (SNAPSHOT_TIME '...')`. Change feed: `FROM db.table_changes('tbl', start, end)` with bounds as snapshot ids or timestamps, returning snapshot_id, rowid, change_type (insert, update_preimage, update_postimage, delete). This is a ready implementation of Adele's knowledge time: each fetch is a snapshot, as_of=<ts> maps to AT (TIMESTAMP), and "what changed since my last pull" maps to table_changes. It would replace the hand-made fetched_at column and part of the revision policy. The catalog file also lists every data file, so a pull is: download the .ducklake file, then fetch the data files that are missing locally. Gaps: the publication guide only covers public buckets ("without authentication") and uploads with rclone; the FAQ says that authentication is delegated to the catalog database. Whether an HTTP bearer secret protects a frozen lake behind a proxy is plausible (it goes through httpfs) but not documented and not verified. Units, grain and refresh ETA still need the Frictionless descriptor.
projects.status: MIT (not re-checked on the repo), v1.0 on 2026-04-13 with DuckDB 1.5.2 (verified on ducklake.select). v1.1 release not verified.

projects.name: rclone (HTTP backend)
projects.what: General file sync tool; its HTTP remote syncs from a web server that returns a parseable directory listing.
projects.overlap: `adele pull`: incremental sync of Parquet partitions to local disk.
projects.takeaways: Verified: works with nginx, Apache and Caddy listings; `rclone sync remote:dir /local/dir`; custom headers with `--http-headers` (an Authorization header can be set; the Bearer format is my inference); the remote is read-only. Weak point: "No checksums are stored" and modification times are accurate to 1 second, so change detection rests on size + mtime. For partitions that are rewritten in place (overwrite policy, current month) this is fragile. A manifest with sha256 or size per partition, written by the server after each fetch and compared by the client, is more reliable and avoids an external binary on each team member's machine. rclone remains a zero-code fallback and is the tool that DuckLake's guide uses to publish.
projects.status: MIT, very active (not re-checked); only the HTTP backend page was read.

projects.name: Hardcharger (GizmoData)
projects.what: Open-source standalone server for DuckDB 2.0, announced 2026-10-21, successor of GizmoSQL. Clients speak Chargewire, an HTTP/1.1 protocol with Arrow IPC results and JSON control messages.
projects.overlap: Authenticated remote query with users and roles, HTTP API usable from curl (the fallback of the skill), Python client.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the vendor page: Apache-2.0 with no paid edition; bearer tokens; users, roles, GRANT/REVOKE in SQL, row policies, column masking; clients: Python ADBC (`adbc-driver-hardcharger`), JDBC, JavaScript, a `hardcharger` CLI, dbt, and an MCP server; Docker image ghcr.io/gizmodata/hardcharger. A Hackernoon article says that an OpenAPI 3.1 description is served at /chargewire/v1/openapi.json and that plain curl can run queries (no curl example seen). It is the only candidate with real per-user grants and a curl-friendly SQL endpoint out of the box. Risks: three weeks old, single vendor, version numbers on the page are inconsistent (2.0.0, 2.5.0, 2.11.0), one benchmark is labelled 2.0.0-rc.1. It does nothing for pull. Wait before depending on it; Quack covers the same need with less risk.
projects.status: Apache-2.0, announced 2026-10-21 (vendor page and one third-party article). GitHub repo https://github.com/gizmodata/hardcharger not opened; maturity not verified.

projects.name: GizmoSQL
projects.what: Arrow Flight SQL server with DuckDB (or SQLite) as the engine, with TLS, password and JWT authentication.
projects.overlap: Authenticated remote SQL over DuckDB.
projects.takeaways: Verified: the README states that GizmoSQL is in maintenance mode and recommends Hardcharger. Core is Apache-2.0 but per-catalog permissions, SSO, session instrumentation and statement queuing were enterprise-only. Default is one user (`gizmosql_user`) with a password; multi-user support is not described. No read-only flag is documented. Flight SQL needs gRPC and an ADBC driver, which is heavier for an agent than HTTP. Do not start a new project on it.
projects.status: Apache-2.0 core, maintenance mode (verified on README, November 2026). Bundles DuckDB 1.5.6 / 2.0.0 edge.

projects.name: DuckDB httpserver community extension (Query.Farm)
projects.what: Community extension that exposes a DuckDB instance as an HTTP API: POST a SQL query, get results; includes a browser query UI.
projects.overlap: HTTP API as fallback for agents without the CLI (curl + key).
projects.takeaways: Verified: auth by HTTP Basic (`user:pass`) or one `X-API-Key` header, or none; DuckDB clients can call it with an HTTP secret and EXTRA_HTTP_HEADERS; builds listed for DuckDB 1.4.x, 1.5.x and 2.0.0; repo moved to https://github.com/Query-farm/httpserver. Only one shared key, so per-member keys must be checked in the reverse proxy. No read-only mode in the extension: the project advises to run DuckDB with -readonly. Good for a curl fallback with almost no code, since Quack does not serve non-DuckDB clients.
projects.status: Community extension, maintainers lmangani, akvlad, niclashaderer, gropaul, rustyconover (verified). License and last release not checked.

projects.name: Delta Sharing (protocol + reference server)
projects.what: Open REST protocol for read-only sharing of Delta/Parquet tables with bearer-token profiles; the server returns presigned URLs of Parquet files. Python connector with `load_as_pandas`.
projects.overlap: Authenticated read-only sharing, incremental reads (change data feed), a list of tables to discover.
projects.takeaways: Verified: Apache-2.0; the reference server is "not a completed implementation of secure web server" and is meant for development; bearer token is optional in the server YAML; storage backends are S3, Azure, GCS and R2 (local filesystem is not mentioned, so a single Linux box would need MinIO or Garage in addition); incremental reads with `load_table_changes_as_pandas` between versions. Two DuckDB community extensions exist (duckdb_delta_sharing by prequel-co, duck_delta_share), maintenance not checked. Too many parts for a dozen datasets. Ideas worth copying: the profile file (endpoint + bearer token in one small JSON given to each member) and the share/schema/table listing endpoints.
