projects.name: Seafowl (Splitgraph)
projects.what: Rust analytical database on DataFusion built for queries over HTTP, with results that follow HTTP cache rules so that a CDN can serve repeated queries.
projects.overlap: HTTP query API; caching of identical agent queries.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the README: "Seafowl's query execution API follows HTTP cache semantics"; write access is a config value (SEAFOWL__FRONTEND__HTTP__WRITE_ACCESS); queries go to POST /q; no limits are stated. The read-access modes (any, password, off) and the ETag mechanism that I remember could not be verified on the page. Idea for Adele: cache `query` results by (SQL hash, catalog version), which also reduces load from agents that repeat the same query. Low priority for ten users.

results.angle_summary: No project that I found ships the history of bidding zones as a table with validity intervals. entsoe-py has only a README table by year and a date-aware geometry loader. Adele must author a small `zones` reference dataset itself (EIC, short name, area type, timezone, valid_from, valid_to, predecessor), seeded from entsoe-py, electricitymaps and the ENTSO-E code list. Challenge to the spec: "units per field" is not sufficient. Each field also needs (1) aggregation (mean power over the interval, or energy per interval), (2) the timestamp label (period start), (3) a sign convention for flows and imbalances, (4) currency, (5) the code list that the values belong to. OEMetadata 2.0 already names two of these (alignment, aggregationType) and is Frictionless-based: copy its keys into the "adele:" block. Resolution must be allowed per row or per period, because 15-minute SDAC (delivery day 2025-10-01) made series mixed. Use pint-parseable unit strings as PUDL does; QUDT and OEO are optional URIs.

projects.name: entsoe-py (EnergieID)
projects.what: Python client for the ENTSO-E Transparency Platform API. Its mappings.py is the de facto reusable table of area codes and ENTSO-E code lists in Python.
projects.overlap: EIC codes of bidding zones, timezones per zone, PSR / business / document / process type code lists, neighbours, history of zones.
projects.takeaways: Verified in entsoe/mappings.py: an `Area` enum where each member holds (EIC code, meaning, tz), for example DE_AT_LU = 10Y1001A1001A63L, DE_LU = 10Y1001A1001A82H, IT_NORD = 10Y1001A1001A73I, all with an IANA timezone. Dicts PSRTYPE_MAPPINGS, DOCSTATUS, BSNTYPE, MARKETAGREEMENTTYPE, DOCUMENTTYPE, PROCESSTYPE, and NEIGHBOURS (keyed by area name). No validity interval per zone in the mapping: the README only has a table by year (DE_AT_LU valid 2015 to 2018, DE_LU and AT from 2018). Some names are aliases of the same EIC (LU_BZN = DE_LU code), so EIC --> name is not one-to-one. The subpackage entsoe/geo has geojson per bidding zone and `load_zones(zones, date)` which 'automatically selects the configuration that was active on the given date' (best effort, not all zones). For Adele: generate the seed of a `zones` reference table and of `codelist_*` tables from mappings.py, then add valid_from / valid_to by hand. The README requires timezone-aware timestamps and does not document mixed resolutions (not found on the pages that I read).
projects.status: MIT. Active. Latest release on the GitHub releases page: v0.8.1, dated 04 Sep (year not shown on the page, probably 2026; not confirmed). PyPI page could not be loaded.

projects.name: ENTSO-E EDI Library: code list, SKOS code list, CIM XSD package, ESMP
projects.what: The official source of the ENTSO-E code lists (PSR types, business types, document types, process types, curve types, units, currencies, coding schemes) and of the CIM European Style Market Profile (IEC 62325-351 and 62325-451-x).
projects.overlap: Authoritative vocabulary for every coded field of ENTSO-E data, and the rule that maps (period start, resolution, position) to a timestamp.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the page: the code list is downloadable as a zip (link named CodelistV96.zip, while the news item of 2026-06-10 says 'Version 95', so the page is inconsistent), as a SKOS zip (ENTSO-E SKOS codelist.zip, machine-readable RDF) and inside a CIM XSD package (CIM_xsd_package_v2026.7z). The page lists IEC 62325-301, -351, -450, -451-1 to -451-8 (451-6 = transparency publications) and the Manual of Procedures v3.3. The IEC texts are paywalled (only previews are linked). The curve type document (found by search, not fetched) gives the rule TimeStepPosition = start of timeInterval + (Position - 1) * Resolution, and curve type A03 (variable sized block) means that a missing position repeats the previous value. For Adele: a fetcher that converts the XSD or SKOS code list into one Parquet table `codelists(list, code, title, definition, codelist_version)`, and each coded field of a descriptor points to its list. Normalizers must forward-fill A03 series before writing Parquet and must record this in the descriptor.
projects.status: Official ENTSO-E page, maintained (news item dated 2026-06-10). Licence of the code list not verified (a search result says Creative Commons for the reference code list; not confirmed on the page). Contents of the zips not opened.

projects.name: OEMetadata (Open Energy Platform)
projects.what: A JSON metadata standard for energy datasets, 'based on the Frictionless Data Package specifications', with ontology annotations per field.
projects.overlap: The Adele catalog descriptor: units per field, time resolution, label alignment, kind of aggregation, annotations of fields and of values.
projects.takeaways: Verified in metadata_key_description.md and example.json (version 2.0): the temporal block has timeseries keys start, end, resolutionValue, resolutionUnit, alignment ('whether timestamps in a time series are to the left, right or in the centre') and aggregationType ('whether the values are a sum, an average or a current value'). Each field has name, description, type, nullable, unit (example 'MW', free string), isAbout (array of {name, @id} with OEO URIs) and valueReference (maps a value of the column, for example 'onshore', to an OEO class). For Adele: reuse the key names alignment and aggregationType in the 'adele:' block, at field level rather than dataset level, because one table can hold MW (average) and MWh (sum). aggregationType = average versus sum is exactly the distinction between mean power and energy per interval. valueReference is a good pattern for enum columns (psr_type B16 --> Solar). Weak points: unit is a free string, resolution is one value per dataset (cannot express a change from 60 to 15 minutes), no sign convention, no currency key.
projects.status: Code MIT, schema and examples CC0-1.0. Version 2.0 is the 'latest' on the production branch. Release date not found on the pages.

projects.name: PUDL metadata system (Catalyst Cooperative)
projects.what: The metadata layer of the Public Utility Data Liberation project (US energy data, published as Parquet and SQLite): field definitions are shared across tables and units are validated.
projects.overlap: Catalog authoring: one definition per field name, units that a machine can parse, code tables for categorical columns, primary key as the grain.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the page: fields are defined once in pudl.metadata.fields.FIELD_METADATA with keys type, description, unit, constraints (enum or pattern), so fields with the same name share one definition, with per-table overrides in FIELD_METADATA_BY_RESOURCE. The unit 'must be parseable by pudl.metadata.units.PUDL_UNIT_REGISTRY, a Pint registry extended with energy-industry units', with compound units such as 'MMBtu / MWh'. Each resource has schema.fields, primary_key (tested for uniqueness when written) and foreign_key_rules; categorical data goes to coding tables. For Adele: (1) a shared dictionary of fields in git (delivery_start, bidding_zone, price_eur_mwh ...) referenced by the dataset yaml files, (2) a CI test that parses every unit with a pint registry extended with EUR, GBP and MTU, (3) the grain expressed as a primary key that the server tests at every refresh. The page does not describe an export to Frictionless (not verified).
projects.status: Open source, docs 'latest' online in November 2026. Licence and last release not checked on this page.

projects.name: electricitymaps-contrib zone configs
projects.what: One YAML file per zone (DE.yaml, DK-DK1.yaml, AU-NSW.yaml ...) that holds reference data for the Electricity Maps parsers, plus the geometries of the zones.
projects.overlap: Reference data per zone: timezone, currency, values with a start date, geometry of bidding zones.
projects.takeaways: Verified in config/zones/DE.yaml: top-level keys include timezone (Europe/Berlin), currency, country, bounding_box, parsers (consumption: ENTSOE.fetch_consumption, price: NORDPOOL.fetch_price), sources, capacity and emissionFactors. Time-varying values are lists of records {datetime, source, value}: each record applies from its datetime until the next one (only a start date, no end date), and each record carries its source. For Adele: this pattern (list of dated records with a source, in a YAML file in git) is the simplest way to store slowly changing reference data such as zone membership or resolution per zone; convert it to closed-open intervals at build time. Zone keys are their own scheme (DK-DK1, not EIC), so a mapping table to EIC is needed. The sign convention of exchanges (sorted zone keys) was not verified: the wiki page was empty and the README does not describe it.
projects.status: AGPL-3.0 since v1.5.0 (older contributions MIT), so copy the ideas and facts, not the files, unless AGPL is acceptable. Active (6,922 commits on master; date of last commit not shown).

projects.name: Open Energy Ontology (OEO)
projects.what: A domain ontology for energy system analysis (OWL), used by OEMetadata to annotate fields and values with stable URIs.
projects.overlap: Stable identifiers for concepts such as 'nameplate capacity', 'wind farm', and (not verified) market concepts and bidding zones.
projects.takeaways: Verified: dual licence CC0-1.0 or MIT, distributed as oeo-full.owl and oeo-closure.owl, source in Manchester syntax, classes cited as label + ID (for example 'energy system' OEO_00030024). In the OEMetadata example, isAbout points to OEO IDs such as OEO_00230003 (nameplate capacity). For Adele: an optional `is_about` URI per field costs little and removes ambiguity for terms such as load versus consumption or gross versus net capacity. I did not verify that OEO has classes for bidding zone, day-ahead price or imbalance; check the TIB terminology service before relying on it. An agent gains more from a one-line definition in the descriptor than from the URI alone.
projects.status: CC0-1.0 or MIT. Active: latest release v2.14.0 dated 08 October (year not shown, after v2.13.0 of 2026-07-10, so probably 2026).

projects.name: Open Power System Data: time series data package
projects.what: A Frictionless data package of load, generation and day-ahead prices for European zones, built from ENTSO-E Transparency data.
projects.overlap: Conventions for time (label, UTC and local), mixed resolutions, naming of bidding zones, Frictionless descriptor for the same sources.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the page: two timestamp columns, utc_timestamp ('start of timeperiod in Coordinated Universal Time') and cet_cest_timestamp (start of period in local time with offset), which removes the ambiguity of the days with 23 or 25 hours. One file per resolution (15 min, 30 min, 60 min) instead of mixing resolutions in one table. Units stated per field (MW for load, generation and capacity; EUR for prices, except the GB price in GBP). Zone names follow the entsoe-py style (DE_LU, IT_NORD) in the column names. For Adele: keep delivery_start in UTC as the key and derive the local delivery day in a view or a documented column; decide explicitly between 'one table per resolution' (OPSD) and 'one long table with delivery_start + delivery_end or a resolution column' (better after the 15-minute change). The wide format with zone and currency in the column name is the pattern to avoid for agents.
projects.status: Stale: latest version 2020-10-06, data until mid-2020. Licence not stated on the page that I read.

projects.name: SDAC 15-minute market time unit (primary announcements)
projects.what: Not a software project: the announcements of the power exchanges about the move of the single day-ahead coupling to a 15-minute market time unit. Listed because it is the reference fact for mixed resolutions.
projects.overlap: Time conventions: resolution of day-ahead data changes inside one dataset.
projects.takeaways: From the search results (EPEX, OTE, HUPX, Nord Pool pages; I did not fetch the pages themselves): go-live on trading day 2025-09-30 for delivery day 2025-10-01, after a postponement from 2025-06-11, in all bidding zones and borders of SDAC; products of 15, 30 and 60 minutes coexist. For Adele: 'resolution' in the 'adele:' block cannot be a single ISO 8601 duration per dataset. Store resolution as a list of validity intervals (per zone if needed), and store delivery_start and delivery_end (half-open) in every row so that a query never has to guess. The descriptor should warn that an hourly price after 2025-10-01 is a derived quantity (an average of four quarter-hours, or a 60-minute product), and which one the dataset holds.
projects.status: Facts from search result summaries of several exchange pages, consistent with each other. Pages not fetched individually. The encoding on the Transparency Platform (PT15M and PT60M periods in one document) was not verified.

projects.name: entsoeapi (R, krose)
projects.what: R client for the ENTSO-E Transparency Platform with functions that download the official EIC code lists as tables.
projects.overlap: EIC reference data as tables: areas, parties, tie lines, resource objects.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the article: functions area_eic(), party_eic(), tie_line_eic(), resource_object_eic(), etc. download per-type files (Y_eicCodes.csv, X_eicCodes.csv, Z_, T_, V_, W_, A_) and all_approved_eic() returns 11 columns (eic_code, eic_display_name, eic_long_name, eic_parent, eic_responsible_party, eic_status, ..., eic_type_function_list, type). all_allocated_eic() downloads a file of about 70 MB with revision_number and doc_status. This shows that ENTSO-E publishes per-type CSV files of approved EIC codes that a fetcher can ingest; the exact URLs are not on the page (read them in the package source). No validity dates in the approved list, so the history of zones still has to be authored. The article contradicts itself on which letter means which type, so take the type letters from ENTSO-E directly. A separate article 'time series restructuring' (not fetched) covers curve types.

projects.name: PyPSA-Eur: build_bidding_zones rule
projects.what: A rule of the PyPSA-Eur workflow that builds one geojson of European bidding zones by merging the shapes of electricitymaps-contrib and of entsoe-py.
projects.overlap: Geometry of bidding zones as a reusable file; evidence about which sources the modelling community trusts.

projects.name: Transparency Energy Knowledge Graph (TEKG, Ontotext)
projects.what: A 2022 research project that converted ENTSO-E Transparency Platform data to an RDF knowledge graph, with a glossary and a specification of the model.
projects.overlap: A semantic model of the same data: EIC areas, ENTSO-E code lists, CIM market profiles, validation of data quality.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the glossary page: made by Ontotext (Sirma AI), funded by the INTERRFACE open call (H2020 grant 824330), glossary last updated 2022-09-28, references IEC 62325, CIM market profiles, EIC area codes, ENTSO-E Codelist v80, and uses RDF, SPARQL, SHACL and DQV. No link to a code repository on the page; QUDT is not mentioned. For Adele: the glossary and the spec page (spec.html, not fetched) are a compact reading list of the ENTSO-E source documents and of the area types. The approach itself (RDF + SPARQL) is heavier than needed for a dozen tables read through DuckDB.

projects.name: QUDT, UCUM and pint (unit vocabularies)
projects.what: Three ways to write a unit so that a machine can read it: QUDT (RDF ontology with URIs per unit), UCUM (a string grammar, used in data exchange), pint (Python registry that parses unit strings; pint-pandas for DataFrame dtypes).
projects.overlap: 'Units per field' in the catalog.
projects.takeaways: Verified: QUDT is CC BY 4.0, distributed as OWL and SHACL Turtle and resolvable URIs, README updated 2026-10-13; whether it has MW-HR and EUR-per-MWh units was not verified. UCUM is at version 2.2 (2024-06-17); megawatt is 'MW' and megawatt hour is 'MW.h' (with the mandatory dot); the part of the spec that I read does not cover currencies. pint: PUDL proves that a pint registry extended with domain units works as a validator of metadata; the pint landing page and the pint-pandas README did not confirm custom currency units (known from memory that `ureg.define('EUR = [currency]')` works, not verified here). For Adele: store `unit` as a pint-parseable string ('MW', 'MWh', 'EUR / MWh') and validate it in CI; this is cheap and agents read it directly. Add the currency as a separate field attribute as well (ISO 4217), because no unit vocabulary handles currency well and GB prices are in GBP. None of the three says whether MW is an instantaneous value or a mean over the interval: this needs the separate aggregation attribute.
projects.status: QUDT: CC BY 4.0, active (README 2026-10-13), release number not found. UCUM 2.2 of 2024-06-17, own licence (terms not read). pint and pint-pandas: versions not found on the pages fetched.

projects.name: ENTSO-E Detailed Data Descriptions and Manual of Procedures
projects.what: The official definition of each data item of the Transparency Platform (total load, day-ahead prices, physical flows, net positions, imbalance prices and volumes ...), part of the Manual of Procedures.
projects.overlap: Source text for field descriptions, units, and sign or direction conventions of each ENTSO-E dataset.
projects.takeaways: Verified (pages 1 to 8 of the PDF read): the copy at this URL is Version 1 Release 4 of 2014-02-24, 69 pages, one section per data item (3.2 total load per market time unit, 3.8 day-ahead prices, net positions, physical flows, 3.13 imbalance prices and total imbalance volume), with definitions (resolution = 'the time difference between successive data values in a time series', capacities 'expressed in megawatts (MW)'). I did not read the sections on flows and imbalances, so the sign conventions are not verified from this document. From search summaries only: the EU balancing rules define a negative imbalance as a shortage of the balance responsible party and a positive one as a surplus; cross-border queries return one direction per (in_Domain, out_Domain) pair, so flows are non-negative per direction and a net flow is a derived quantity. For Adele: quote the relevant paragraph of this document in each descriptor (with article number of Regulation 543/2013), and make `sign_convention` a mandatory field attribute for flows, net positions and imbalances (for example 'positive = export from in_zone to out_zone').
projects.status: Official ENTSO-E document. This copy is old (2014); the EDI library lists a MoP v3.3 zip which should contain the current version (not opened). The current knowledge base on transparencyplatform.zendesk.com returned HTTP 403.

projects.what: A newer Python client for the ENTSO-E Transparency Platform whose package structure mirrors the official API documentation (for example entsoe.Market.EnergyPrices for item 12.1.D).
projects.overlap: Alternative fetcher for the ENTSO-E API; naming of datasets after the official article numbers.

One idea for Adele: name or tag each dataset with the article of Regulation 543/2013 (12.1.D, 6.1.A ...) as this package does, since this identifier is stable across the ENTSO-E documentation, the API guide and the web interface, and an agent can use it to find the official definition.

results.angle_summary: Main challenge to the spec: licences are per dataset and several are not open. Per a third-party reading of ENTSO-E's free re-use list (primary page returned 403), day-ahead prices, actual load and generation per type are NOT on the CC-BY 4.0 list. JAO terms (read) allow only "own internal purposes", forbid making content available to third parties, and forbid sharing the API token. Energy-Charts prices are "private and internal use only" outside 16 SMARD zones. So Adele is defensible as a mirror inside one organisation, not across organisations. Add to each descriptor: licence, attribution string, redistribution scope. Ingestion: use the ENTSO-E File Library (SFTP is discontinued), not the REST API. For the ETA of the next refresh, JAO itself recommends polling its monitoring/metadata endpoints around deadlines. No complete Parquet mirror exists. hsilvosa/entsoe-observatory is the closest prior art; Ember and Energinet are clean CC-BY backfills.

projects.name: ENTSO-E Transparency Platform (terms of use, free re-use list, File Library, API rate limit)
projects.what: The primary source for most Adele datasets. Governed by General Terms and Conditions plus a separate 'List of Data Available for Free Re-use' (CC-BY 4.0) published at https://transparencyplatform.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/40921911218961-Legal-Terms-and-Conditions.
projects.overlap: Licence field of the catalog, fetchers (bulk channel), rate limits, revision policy, per-user API keys.
projects.takeaways: READ IN THE PDF (version approved 8 Nov 2018, clause II.2.5): the user must act in good faith, must 'mention the ENTSO-E Transparency Platform as the source of publication of the data', must not suggest endorsement, and must not prejudice the copyright of the 'Primary Owner of Data'. ENTSO-E publishes a list of data that can be re-used without the owner's agreement, and 'the Data User has responsibility to check this list before each re-use'. Clause 7: the web GUI is not for robots, and ENTSO-E may add technical constraints. NOT VERIFIED ON THE PRIMARY PAGE (Zendesk returns 403), from search snippets and from entsoemcp.com/licensing: the list (version 18 Oct 2023) is CC-BY 4.0 and covers e.g. imbalance prices, physical flows, day-ahead NTC, day-ahead load forecast, but NOT day-ahead prices, actual load, generation per type, wind/solar forecasts, installed capacity, outages, scheduled exchanges. Consequence for Adele: an internal mirror with attribution fits the terms, but redistribution outside the organisation of the items that are not on the list needs the agreement of the primary owner (power exchanges for prices). Rate limit (search snippet of the help centre, not opened): 400 requests per minute per API token, with an IP ban policy. Bulk channel: the File Library replaced SFTP (SFTP planned end was Sept 2025, then 20 Nov 2025 per a migration notice seen in a search snippet; new extracts carry an _r3 suffix; new platform went live around 12 Nov 2025). File Library needs a token from username/password, and the password expires every 183 days (snippet): plan an alert for this in the fetcher. Publication deadlines per data item are in the Detailed Data Descriptions PDF (https://eepublicdownloads.entsoe.eu/clean-documents/mc-documents/transparency-platform/MOP/DetailedDescriptionDocument.pdf, 69 pages, downloaded but not parsed).
projects.status: Terms PDF read directly (2018 version; entsoemcp cites a 29 March 2023 version that I did not open). Free re-use list, rate limit and SFTP dates: NOT verified on primary pages (403), secondary sources only. MoP v3.4 dated 10 Nov 2023 per ACER.

projects.name: JAO Publication Tool (PuTo) and JAO terms of use
projects.what: Source of flow-based domain data, capacities and auction results for Core, Nordic and Italy North. JAO published access parameters in Oct/Nov 2025 and has General Terms and Conditions for the Use of the Information Systems.
projects.overlap: Licence field, fetcher design, 'ETA of next refresh', per-user API keys.
projects.takeaways: READ IN THE JAO PDF (https://www.jao.eu/sites/default/files/news_media/PuTo%20Communication.pdf): rate limit of 100 requests per minute per user or IP; default responses contain up to two business days of data; history stays available with date and time filters; JAO asks users to call the 'monitoring and metadata API endpoints to check data freshness before performing large requests' and to query around publication deadlines, not to poll continuously. This is a ready pattern for Adele's freshness and ETA fields. READ ON https://new-prod.jao.eu/terms-conditions: rights are 'non-exclusive, non-sublicensable, non-transferable' and limited to 'Legitimate Use', which includes use 'for its own internal purposes'. Content cannot be 'made available to any third party' or commercialised without written authorisation. Bots are prohibited, the API token 'under no circumstance can be shared or transferred', training ML models on the content needs prior authorisation, and the source must be mentioned. Consequence: an Adele mirror is defensible only inside one legal entity; per-user Adele keys do not replace JAO's own conditions; ask JAO if the team spans organisations. The ML clause matters if the team trains forecasting models on JAO data.
projects.status: News page and PDF read (PDF dated 13 Nov 2025). Terms read on new-prod.jao.eu (a JAO host; I did not check that the same text is on www.jao.eu). No go-live date for the limits is stated.

projects.name: Energy-Charts API (Fraunhofer ISE)
projects.what: Public JSON API for German and European generation, load and day-ahead prices. It publishes an llms.txt file for agents and returns a licence field in each response.
projects.overlap: Licence per dataset, rate limits, prior art for describing an API to agents (llms.txt), freshness fields.
projects.takeaways: Verified in llms.txt and openapi.json: default licence is CC BY 4.0 with attribution to energy-charts.info, 'unless the response's license field states otherwise'. Day-ahead prices are licensed per bidding zone: CC BY 4.0 from 'Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de' for AT, BE, CH, CZ, DE-LU, DE-AT-LU, DK1, DK2, FR, HU, IT-North, NL, NO2, PL, SE4, SI ('published without changes'); all other zones are 'for private and internal use only', and external or commercial use is prohibited (users are sent to EPEX SPOT). Rate limits are low: default 2 requests per minute (burst 4), price 2 per minute (burst 2), signal 20 per minute, adjusted to server load, HTTP 429 with Retry-After. So it is not a bulk channel. Design ideas for Adele: (1) licence can vary inside one dataset (by zone), so the descriptor needs a licence per partition or per zone, not only per dataset; (2) responses carry generated_at, available_from, available_until, which is close to Adele's freshness and coverage fields; (3) llms.txt as a cheap entry point next to SKILL.md.

projects.name: SMARD (Bundesnetzagentur)
projects.what: German regulator's market data portal. It republishes ENTSO-E data after verification, with a download centre and an undocumented JSON endpoint.
projects.overlap: Clean licence for prices of DE and neighbouring zones, attribution wording, revision behaviour.

Adele should store the licence with a checked_at date. SMARD is the legally cleanest channel for day-ahead prices of the 16 zones listed by Energy-Charts. No official API documentation or rate limit found; a user manual (04/2026) exists as PDF and was not read.

projects.name: hsilvosa/entsoe-observatory
projects.what: A one-person, low-cost data platform: ENTSO-E day-ahead prices (A44) and actual load (A65) for 51 bidding zones from 2015, with Open-Meteo weather and ECB rates, in Hive-partitioned zstd Parquet on Cloudflare R2, with DuckDB as the main engine. Published on Hugging Face.
projects.overlap: Server side almost one to one: fetchers, Parquet layout, DuckDB, revisions, schema contracts, data quality.
projects.takeaways: Verified in README and HF card (https://huggingface.co/datasets/hsilvosa/entsoe-observatory): layers landing (immutable files with sha256) --> bronze (parsed rows with lineage: source file, checksum, document id, revision, run id) --> silver (typed, deduplicated) --> gold (nine tables, each with a versioned JSON contract in contracts/gold/). Business key (dataset, zone, timestamp_utc, resolution, sequence). Revisions: 'the newest revision of a document wins; late revisions can be cut off at a snapshot time', and native tables keep revision_number: this is Adele's as_of query, built from ENTSO-E's own revision numbers plus a cutoff. Partition key is year (Adele plans delivery month). Schedules in UTC: load hourly, prices at 11:25 and 13:25, weekly data quality run. Hourly tables keep slots_present and slots_expected to handle the change to 15-minute resolution. HF licence tag is the custom 'entsoe-reuse-with-attribution' and the card tells users to check ENTSO-E's free re-use list before redistributing, which shows that the author did not resolve the licence question for prices. Known gaps documented (PL prices 697 days, IE_SEM load missing since 2025-10): useful as a checklist for backfill tests. Uses the REST API, not the File Library.

projects.name: Swissgrid grid data (Energy Statistic Switzerland, control area balance)
projects.what: Swiss TSO publications: one XLSX per year with 15-minute aggregates (2009 to 2026), plus CSV/XLSX files for control area balance and total system imbalance.
projects.overlap: Source for an xlsx fetcher; documented publication schedule and revision behaviour (inputs for 'ETA of next refresh' and revision policy).
projects.takeaways: Verified on the page: the energy statistic is 'initially published periodical every 15th working day after the end of the previous month', and corrections are published monthly. Data are provisional and 'reliable from 6 months onwards', because the partners that deliver the data can still claim changes. So this dataset needs the append-only revision policy with fetched_at, a refresh rule expressed in working days (not a cron interval), and a 'provisional until' field of 6 months in the descriptor. Files for 2009-2019 are XLS, later ones XLSX (two parsers). Control area balance and imbalance values are 'not legally binding' and come from real-time systems. No licence is stated on the page, only a liability exclusion: treat as internal use with source mention until Swissgrid's legal information page is checked. BFE republishes Swissgrid-based series on opendata.swiss under open terms with source required (search snippet, not opened), which may be the cleaner channel.

projects.name: PUDL (Catalyst Cooperative) + its agent skills (pudl, datapackage)
projects.what: Open pipeline for US energy data (EIA, FERC, EPA) that publishes Parquet on public S3 with a Frictionless Data Package v2 descriptor, plus an official agent skill (https://github.com/catalyst-cooperative/agent-skills) that teaches coding agents to find tables, read column metadata and load the Parquet.
projects.overlap: Almost the whole Adele design except the bitemporal axis and the 15-minute refresh: fetchers --> Parquet --> DuckDB, Frictionless descriptor as catalog, SKILL.md as agent interface, no MCP.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the pages. (1) Catalog: one pudl_parquet_datapackage.json for all tables, with column types, constraints and foreign keys. The agent queries it with jq and never loads it whole. (2) Skill layout: SKILL.md + references/ + scripts/ + assets/. A script fetch_descriptor.py caches the descriptor locally and reuses it if it is less than one day old. Small JSON assets are queried before the long markdown references (progressive disclosure). (3) Rules in SKILL.md worth copying: 'always surface usage warnings from the descriptor before giving loading code', run a broad keyword search of the catalog before answering 'do we have data on X', flag answers that come from recall, check schema.foreignKeys before a join, estimate the table size before an unfiltered load. (4) The skill is split in two: a generic 'datapackage' skill (works for any Frictionless descriptor, reads CSV, Parquet, DuckDB, SQLite) and a domain skill 'pudl' that depends on it. Adele could reuse the generic datapackage skill as is. (5) Two channels: 'nightly' (ephemeral, less validated) and quarterly 'stable' releases versioned by date and archived on Zenodo. (6) Failure modes they document: dots in the S3 bucket name break DuckDB's default S3 addressing (need URL_STYLE 'path'); ambient AWS credentials must be cleared for a public bucket; a 100 GB dataset (FERC EQR) cannot be versioned, so only one version is public; SQLite output is deprecated and stops in 2027 (Parquet is the recommended format, DuckDB file is built from the Parquet). (7) They also ship skill evaluations (pages 'Skill Evals' and 'Datapackage Evals' exist in the docs, content not read).

projects.name: Grid Status (hosted API, dataset metadata, publish-time model, Snowflake listing)
projects.what: Commercial US power market data service (about 500 datasets from the ISOs) with a REST API, a Python client, a Snowflake Marketplace listing, and docs published as llms.txt and per-page markdown for agents.
projects.overlap: Catalog fields per dataset (coverage, freshness, status, primary key, time columns) and the query semantics for forecast vintages (delivery time against publication time).
projects.takeaways: Verified. (1) Dataset metadata object (https://docs.gridstatus.io/developers/api-reference/dataset-metadata): earliest_available_time_utc, latest_available_time_utc, last_checked_time_utc, primary_key_columns, time_index_column, publish_time_column, subseries_index_column, data_frequency, publication_frequency, number_of_rows_approximate, status (active, deprecated, retired), all_columns (name, type). There is no unit field: this is a gap that Adele's per-field units close. (2) Publish-time query modes go further than a single as_of: 'latest' (newest publication per delivery interval), 'latest_report' (only the newest report), an exact timestamp, 'latest_before:<offset>[@HH:MM:SS]' (newest publication at or before a cutoff that is defined relative to each delivery time, for example the day-ahead bid close), and 'window:<offset>' (all publications between the cutoff and delivery). The recipe 'Get Latest Forecast as of Bid Close' exists in the docs. Challenge for Adele: as_of=<fixed timestamp> covers 'what did we know on Monday' but not backtesting, which needs a cutoff relative to each delivery interval. Ship a documented SQL macro or view for that case. (3) Naming convention interval_start_utc, interval_end_utc, publish_time_utc states UTC in the column name. (4) Docs expose llms.txt, llms-full.txt and '.md' versions of each page; there is a 'Dataset Updates' and a 'Dataset Audit' endpoint. (5) No official MCP server appears in their llms.txt; the MCP servers that exist are third-party wrappers.

projects.name: S&P Global Energy: Genie agents + MCP over structured commodity data (Databricks blog, 2026-09-25)
projects.what: Write-up by a data vendor on how it exposed its structured energy data to LLM agents: one narrow text-to-SQL agent per group of tables, each exposed as an MCP server, composed per commodity by a FastMCP proxy.
projects.overlap: Agent interface and catalog curation; the only source found with explicit 'what failed before' statements in the energy domain.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the page. What failed before: hand-built text-to-SQL pipelines ('powerful but brittle': schema changes, ambiguous column names and domain metric definitions each became engineering work); one custom API per use case (new endpoint per question pattern); exports to external AI tools (duplicated data, stale data, loss of governance). One large agent per commodity degraded answer quality, so they keep agents narrow and combine at a higher layer. Lessons they state: invest in descriptions, business definitions and example queries ('separates a demo from a product'); keep a benchmark of test questions with verified answers and rerun it after each change of instructions or data; track how often domain experts agree with the generated SQL; namespace tools clearly. For Adele: add 2 or 3 verified example queries per dataset to the descriptor, and keep a small set of benchmark questions with known answers to test the SKILL.md after each change. The post gives no numeric accuracy and no 'would do differently' section.

projects.name: timedb and EnergyDB (rebase.energy)
projects.what: Open-source Python client and schema for energy time series with three time dimensions (valid_time, knowledge_time, change_time), stored in ClickHouse; EnergyDB adds a Postgres catalog of assets and series with units.
projects.overlap: The bitemporal model (delivery time and knowledge time), append-only revisions, as-of reads.
projects.takeaways: Verified. (1) Three axes, not two: valid_time (delivery), knowledge_time (when the forecast was issued or the value became known) and change_time (when the row was written or corrected). A correction is a new row with the same (series_id, valid_time, knowledge_time). Challenge for Adele: fetched_at mixes two things. For a forecast, the source's own issue time is the knowledge time; fetched_at is only the time the server saw it. Store both when the source provides an issue time, otherwise as_of queries are wrong by the fetch delay and by any backfill. (2) API: read as of a point in time, read_relative() for a per-window day-ahead cutoff, include_knowledge_time=True for the full history. (3) timedb deliberately has no catalog ('no naming, units, or labels to keep in sync'); EnergyDB (https://pypi.org/project/energydb/0.3.0/) adds a TimeSeriesDescriptor with name, unit, data type (ACTUAL or FORECAST) and series type (for example OVERLAPPING). A flag 'overlapping or not' per dataset is a useful descriptor field. (4) Backend changed from PostgreSQL + TimescaleDB (older PyPI text and a fork README) to ClickHouse (current README): the API is not stable. Not a fit as a component for a Parquet + DuckDB design.

projects.takeaways: Verified. (1) Each curve has a curve_type that tells the client which operation to use: TIMESERIES, SCENARIO_TIMESERIES, INSTANCE, PERIODS, PERIOD_INSTANCES, OHLC, TRADES, PPA. Adele's 'revision policy' field plays the same role; consider one explicit enum that the skill maps to a query pattern. (2) An instance = (issued, tag), for example the ECMWF run issued at 00:00 with tag 'ec'. The tag matters: two forecasts with the same issue time from different models must not collide, so the key of an append-only forecast dataset is (zone, delivery_start, issued, source or tag). (3) A resolution is a frequency plus a timezone (UTC, CET, Europe/Gas_Day), with a class that handles daylight saving changes. Daily and monthly products in power markets are defined in local time (CET), so 'UTC + ISO 8601 duration' is not enough for daily data: store the timezone that defines the delivery day. (4) From search snippets only (older doc versions): relative forecast queries (N days ahead, filtered by tag and time of day of issue) and instances.rolling(). Delivery is Excel, API, Python according to Montel's page; no Snowflake, S3 or Parquet delivery and no MCP server was found for Energy Quantified, Montel or Volue.

results.angle_summary: No public write-up was found from an energy trader, utility or TSO (Octopus, Tibber, Statkraft, Axpo, Alpiq, BKW, Vattenfall, Uniper, RWE...) of the full combination (fetchers --> Parquet --> DuckDB + catalog with units and grain + bitemporal + agent interface). Only vendor case studies exist. The closest working system is PUDL: Parquet + Frictionless descriptor + an official agent skill, no MCP. It validates Adele's catalog and skill choices, and its generic "datapackage" skill may be reusable. Commercial vendors (Modo, Energy Aspects, S&P) all chose hosted MCP. Challenges to the spec: (1) a fixed as_of is not enough for backtests; Grid Status offers a cutoff relative to each delivery time; (2) fetched_at is not knowledge time: store the source's issue time and a source tag too; (3) daily products need the timezone that defines the day; (4) add usage warnings, verified example queries, an owner and benchmark questions per dataset.

No ready-made tool covers this angle. Adele should build a small harness of its own from known parts. Proposal: 40 tasks (about 10 easy lookups, 25 "trap" tasks where the wrong timezone, unit, grain or revision gives a different number, 5 tasks that must not use Adele), 5 runs per task and per variant, deterministic comparison of result tables, plus a check of the executed SQL. With 40 tasks, only drops of roughly 15 points or more are detectable on the mean, so add a per-task rule. Challenges to the spec: (1) BuySideFlow found point-in-time violations in 50.8% of runs with a correct result, so the score must also inspect the SQL (as_of present); (2) Vercel measured that a skill was not invoked in 56% of cases, so test triggering; (3) `pull` + local DuckDB leaves no server log, so add client-side query logging; (4) the spec has no query log at all.

projects.name: Miller, 'Adding Error Bars to Evals' (Anthropic, arXiv 2411.00640)
projects.what: Paper with formulas for the uncertainty of an eval score, for the comparison of two variants on the same questions, and for the number of questions and repeats needed.
projects.overlap: Run count per task, scoring rule, and the decision 'is the new SKILL.md worse'.
projects.takeaways: Verified in the HTML version. (1) The unit of analysis is the task, not the run: average the K runs of a task to a pass rate, then compute the standard error over the n task means, SE = sqrt(Var/n). Pooling all K*n runs as if independent understates the error. (2) Compare old vs new on the same tasks by the per-task difference d_i = s_new,i - s_old,i, SE = sqrt(Var(d)/n). This removes the variation due to task difficulty, which is common to both variants. (3) Repeats K reduce only the run-to-run part of the variance; in the paper's example K=2 removes 1/3, K=4 one half, the limit is 2/3, so K beyond about 5 brings little and more tasks bring more. (4) Smallest detectable difference: delta = (1.96+0.84)*sqrt((omega^2 + sigma_A^2/K + sigma_B^2/K)/n) for 5% false alarms and 80% detection; the paper's worked case with n=198 gives 13.2 points at K=1 and 7.5 points at K=10. My own scaling to n=40 (multiply by sqrt(198/40)=2.2, same assumed variances, not from the paper): about 29 points at K=1, about 17 points at K=10. Meaning for Adele: 40 tasks cannot certify a 3-point change; they detect large regressions only. So keep the suite as a regression guard (target near 100% on stable tasks) and add a per-task rule, e.g. flag any task that went from 5/5 to 3/5 or less, then read its transcripts. (5) Do not lower temperature to reduce variance. (6) If several tasks share one dataset or one trap, they are not independent: use clustered standard errors (cluster = dataset).
projects.status: Preprint, November 2024; HTML v1 fetched 2026-11-13. Formulas quoted from the fetched summary of the paper; the n=40 numbers are my derivation.

projects.name: Anthropic engineering: 'Demystifying evals for AI agents'

projects.name: Spider 2.0 evaluation suite (xlang-ai/Spider2)
projects.what: Scoring code of the Spider 2.0 text-to-SQL benchmark: execution accuracy by comparison of the predicted result table with one or several gold tables.
projects.overlap: Scoring rule for `adele query` results.
projects.takeaways: As read by the fetch tool from evaluate.py: score is 1 if every gold column vector equals some column of the prediction; column names are never compared; extra predicted columns are allowed; row counts must match; numbers compared with math.isclose(abs_tol=1e-2); NaN normalized to 0; per-task `condition_cols` (indices of the gold columns that matter) and `ignore_order`; several gold files per task ({id}_a.csv, _b.csv) and a match with any one passes. Good ideas to copy: per-task list of columns that matter, several accepted gold tables for ambiguous questions, tolerance on numbers, ignore names. Things to change for Adele: (a) with ignore_order each column is sorted on its own, so the alignment of rows across columns is lost and a result with values attached to the wrong timestamps can pass; sort whole rows by the key columns instead; (b) an absolute tolerance of 0.01 is wrong for MW vs GW vs EUR/MWh, use a relative tolerance (e.g. 1e-6) so that a unit error of 1000x always fails; (c) NaN = 0 hides missing data, which Adele must distinguish; (d) allow extra columns but require the grain: same number of rows, so double counting after a join fails. Store gold as SQL, not as a CSV, because the data refresh; pin tasks to closed historical periods and, for revised datasets, to a fixed as_of.

projects.name: BuySideFlow (arXiv 2611.12966)
projects.what: November 2026 benchmark of 408 tasks where LLM agents write SQL and SQL-Python workflows on a point-in-time financial database, with an expert audit of the executed workflows.
projects.overlap: Bitemporal correctness: use of revised or current values where point-in-time values were required.
projects.takeaways: Verified in the abstract and HTML: result accuracy 16.2% to 36.8% over nine agent configurations; in an audit of 900 runs on 100 tasks, 193 of the 380 runs that passed the result check (50.8%) contained a point-in-time violation. So a matching result does not prove temporal validity. Taxonomy: A1 confusion of valid time, recording time, disclosure time or cutoff (the most frequent, 49% of an audited sample of 200); A2 current state used instead of historical state (8%); A3 right historical source but wrong handling of validity intervals, version selection, historical joins or deduplication (29%). A rule-based static check of the code reached 94.0% precision but 34.9% recall. Targeted perturbation (simulate a delayed recording) changed the output or caused failure in 58.5% of the flagged runs. Result check: normalized column names, rounding to task precision (default 4 decimals), row multiplicity preserved, order only when required. For Adele: (1) choose point-in-time tasks on delivery periods where a revision really changed the value, so that latest and as_of answers differ (check this when the task is written); (2) also assert on the SQL (as_of or fetched_at filter present) for append-only datasets; (3) include one task per class A1, A2, A3; (4) one run per task at temperature 0 was used there, so the paper gives no guidance on run counts.
projects.status: arXiv preprint dated November 2026, fetched 2026-11-13 (first 100,000 characters of the HTML). No code repository found. Data are licensed, so not reusable.

The number of runs per question is not stated, and the 50% vs 73% comparison rests on one run per arm of 40 questions: by the Miller formulas such a gap is near the limit of what 40 questions can show, so treat it as indicative. Claudeception (https://motherduck.com/blog/claudeception-inside-the-mind-of-an-analytics-agent/): traces of 50 BIRD questions stored in the database and classified by an LLM judge (single-shot 23 traces, 91% success; iterative 25, 64%; struggling 2, 0%). projects.takeaways: Verified on the blog (2026-10-27): failures sorted into five modes (no attempt, wrong plan, wrong data selection, wrong implementation, runtime error) and 16 sub-modes; analysis of the tables each run queried: the top five models queried 78% of the needed dimension tables, the bottom five 49%; 43% of failed runs never read at least one table that the reference SQL uses; the largest group of failures is wrong data selection; the classifier also flagged 18 answers that the grader probably scored wrongly. Negative result worth noting: a hint injected during the run ('you have not looked at table X') left accuracy flat (pooled net +12, 95% interval -18 to +42, i.e. compatible with no effect). For Adele: log, per query, the datasets and columns referenced (DuckDB can return them from the parsed statement) and compare with the gold SQL of the task: 'never read the right dataset', 'never called describe before query', 'did not filter on fetched_at' are computable without an LLM. In production logs (no gold), useful signals are: queries that fail with a binder error (unknown column --> a misleading field name), columns never selected, repeated near-identical queries from the same key within minutes (the agent is searching), aggregates over an append-only dataset without as_of.

projects.name: Vercel: 'AGENTS.md outperforms skills in our agent evals'
projects.what: Vercel eval (27 January 2026) that compared a skill with a compressed documentation index in AGENTS.md for knowledge absent from training data.
projects.overlap: Challenge to the spec choice 'a SKILL.md with progressive disclosure' and the need for a triggering test.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the page: pass rate 53% baseline, 53% with the skill by default, 79% with the skill plus an explicit instruction to use it, 100% with an 8KB index in AGENTS.md; the skill was never invoked in 56% of cases by default; wording mattered ('explore the project first, then invoke the skill' gave better results than 'you MUST invoke the skill'). They also had to harden the eval: remove test leakage, clarify ambiguous prompts, assert on behaviour and not on implementation. For Adele: (1) measure the trigger rate as a separate number, and report accuracy both over all runs and over runs where the skill was loaded, so that a descriptor problem is not confused with a triggering problem; (2) test a variant where a few lines in the project's CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md name Adele and the `adele list` command; this is a cheap arm in the same harness; (3) include tasks that do not name Adele at all ('what was the day-ahead price in CH yesterday?'). Caveat: one framework, models of January 2026; newer models may trigger skills more reliably, which is one more reason to measure.
projects.status: Page fetched 2026-11-13. Number of tasks and of retries not stated in the fetched summary.

projects.name: BIRD Mini-Dev (bird-bench/mini_dev)
projects.what: Small version of the BIRD text-to-SQL benchmark (500 pairs, 780 in V2) with three metrics: execution accuracy, an efficiency score, and Soft F1.
projects.overlap: Scoring rule: alternatives to strict 0/1 execution accuracy.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the README: EX via evaluation_ex.py (definition not given on the page; in the BIRD paper it is equality of the sets of result rows, from memory, not verified here); Soft F1 compares the returned tables cell-wise regardless of column order and computes precision, recall and F1 from matched, predicted-only and gold-only values, to reduce the effect of column order and missing values. For Adele: keep 0/1 as the headline (a wrong number is wrong), and log Soft F1 as a diagnostic that separates 'almost right, one row missing at the interval boundary' from 'completely wrong'. A set-based EX removes duplicate rows, so it cannot see double counting in a detail result: compare as multisets (keep row multiplicity, as BuySideFlow does). Warning from MotherDuck (https://motherduck.com/blog/bird-bench-and-data-models/, seen in search only): 49 of 151 inspected BIRD gold queries were judged wrong, so gold answers of a self-built set need a second reviewer.
projects.status: Active: README lists an annotation update on 2026-10-28. License CC BY-SA 4.0. EX definition and the MotherDuck critique not verified on primary pages.

projects.name: Braintrust
projects.what: Hosted evaluation and tracing platform with a Python/TypeScript SDK (Eval, scorers, experiments, comparison of trials).
projects.overlap: Possible hosted harness and trace viewer; used in the MotherDuck eval.
projects.takeaways: Verified on the docs: `trial_count` (Python) / `trialCount` (TS) runs each input several times, with a per-case override on `EvalCase(trial_count=5)` (useful: more runs on tasks known to be unstable); runs with the same input are grouped; custom scorers are plain Python functions (input, expected, output) --> number; `autoevals` has ready scorers such as NumericDiff. For Adele the value is the trace viewer and the comparison of experiments. Costs: prompts, SQL and results go to a third-party service, which conflicts with the 'small self-hosted' goal; the exact aggregation math is not documented on the page, so standard errors must still be computed by hand.

projects.name: Context-layer ablation on DABStep (arXiv 2609.22259) and Tk-Boost (arXiv 2602.13521)
projects.what: Two papers on what part of the context given to a data agent improves accuracy: an ablation of a YAML 'data contract' on the DABStep benchmark, and a method that derives corrective knowledge from an agent's observed mistakes on a database.
projects.overlap: Design of ablation experiments on the Adele descriptor (which fields earn their tokens) and the loop from failures to descriptor fixes.
projects.takeaways: Verified in the abstracts. 2609.22259: four arms on four models (full contract; scaffolding only with every prose field emptied; same knowledge pasted in the prompt; pre-computed views as a ceiling); the semantic content gave the gain (hard-task accuracy e.g. 13.9% --> 55.1% and 37.0% --> 77.4%), scaffolding alone added 0-5 points on small models and 14-15 on frontier models; knowledge retrieved through the tool was used far more often than the same knowledge pasted in the prompt (up to 98% vs 4% of the generated SQL carried the rule); arms without enforcement submitted 166 mutating statements. For Adele: run the same kind of ablation on the descriptor with the 40 tasks: full descriptor vs without units vs without grain vs without the 5 sample rows vs without the revision policy. Each arm costs 40 x 5 runs; it tells which fields change answers and which only cost tokens. Tk-Boost: let the agent answer labeled queries, analyze its mistakes, write knowledge with conditions of applicability; reports up to +16.9% on Spider 2.0 and +13.7% on BIRD, and says that simply storing past interactions does not remove repeated mistakes (the last point from a search summary). For Adele: each recurrent failure in the eval or in the logs becomes a sentence in the description of the field concerned plus a new task that reproduces it. DABStep scoring (search result only): type-aware comparison of numbers, lists and strings with a numeric tolerance.
projects.status: Both preprints; only abstracts fetched 2026-11-13. Number of tasks, runs and scoring details of 2609.22259 not verified; DABStep tolerance value differs between sources (1e-4 vs 1e-2), not verified.

gaps.question: How do projects that expose a DuckDB (or similar) endpoint accepting arbitrary SQL from remote clients and LLM agents harden it? Cover read-only mode, DuckDB settings (enable_external_access, allowed_directories, lock_configuration, memory_limit, threads, query timeouts), blocking of filesystem and network functions (read_csv, httpfs, ATTACH, COPY, extension install), limits on result size, quotas and rate limits per API key, key issuance and rotation for a small team, audit logs of queries, and process or container isolation. Look for write-ups and incidents from MotherDuck, Datasette (time limits, immutable mode), the DuckDB 'Securing DuckDB' docs, GizmoSQL, the httpserver extension, ROAPI, Seafowl, and from prompt-injection reports where an agent ran hostile SQL. Which minimal set of controls fits one Linux box with about ten trusted users?

Which reference data, vocabularies and conventions does an electricity-market catalog need so that an agent reads fields without ambiguity, and which existing projects encode them in a machine-readable way? Cover: EIC codes and the history of bidding zones (for example the DE-AT-LU split in 2018, Italian and Nordic zone changes) modelled as validity intervals; ENTSO-E code lists (PSR types, business types, document and process types) and IEC 62325 / CIM market profiles; unit vocabularies (QUDT, UCUM, pint, the oemetadata unit and ontology annotations via the Open Energy Ontology) and the distinction between MW (mean power) and MWh per interval; time conventions (period-start versus period-end labels, DST days with 23 or 25 hours, local delivery day versus UTC, the move to the 15-minute market time unit in day-ahead coupling in 2025 and the resulting mixed resolutions); sign conventions for flows and imbalances; currency. Which projects ship these as reusable tables or packages (entsoe-py mappings, electricitymaps zone configs, PyPSA-Eur, OEO, ENTSO-E code list downloads), and how do they document them for users or agents?

For each public source that a European electricity-market data layer would ingest (ENTSO-E Transparency Platform, JAO, EPEX/Nord Pool day-ahead prices as republished, Swissgrid, SMARD, Energy-Charts, Elexon, Open-Meteo, national TSOs), what are (a) the licence and redistribution terms, including whether an internal team mirror with per-user API keys is allowed and which attribution is required, (b) the rate limits and the bulk channels that avoid them (ENTSO-E SFTP and the newer File Library / bulk download API, the 2024-2025 redesign of the Transparency Platform and its API changes, JAO publication tool API), (c) the publication schedules and revision behaviour documented by the source (needed for 'ETA of next refresh' and for the revision policy), and (d) existing third-party mirrors already in Parquet or similar (Hugging Face datasets, Zenodo, Kaggle, AWS Open Data, Ember, OPSD successors, community buckets) that could serve as backfill or as prior art for layout and partitioning?

Who has already built and described an internal 'market data lake for analysts and LLM agents' at an energy trading firm, utility, TSO or energy research group, and what did they learn? Search engineering blogs, conference talks (PyData, EuroPython, DuckCon, Data+AI Summit energy track, Energy Data Space and Open Energy Modelling Initiative workshops, the openmod forum), and 2025-2026 posts from firms such as Octopus/Kraken, Tibber, Statkraft, Axpo, Alpiq, BKW, Vattenfall, Orsted, Uniper, RWE Supply & Trading, Montel, Enappsys, Amperon, Modo, Timera, as well as academic groups (ETH, EPFL, TU Delft, DTU, KIT, Fraunhofer). Look for systems with the same combination: scheduled fetchers --> Parquet --> DuckDB, a catalog with units and grain, bitemporal storage of forecasts and revisions, and an agent interface (skill, CLI, MCP or text-to-SQL). Also check commercial 'bring the data to your lake' offers aimed at this (Snowflake Marketplace and Databricks Marketplace energy listings, Montel/Energy Quantified/Volue delivery to S3 or Parquet, Amphora-like data exchanges). Report architecture, catalog format, failure modes, and what they would do differently.

How should one test that an agent, given the Adele skill and catalog, really answers data questions correctly, and that a change to a descriptor or to SKILL.md does not make results worse? Find concrete methods and tools for small, self-built evaluation sets on a private tabular catalog: Anthropic skill-creator evals and skill triggering tests, Inspect AI, promptfoo, Braintrust, LangSmith, dbt's and MotherDuck's published evaluation setups, the Spider 2.0 / BIRD scoring methods (execution accuracy, comparison of result sets), and write-ups that measure typical agent errors on time-series data (wrong timezone, wrong unit, wrong grain or double counting after a join, use of revised values where point-in-time values were required, stale data taken as fresh). Which question set of about 30-50 tasks, which scoring rule, and which run count per task give a trustworthy signal given that agent runs vary from one run to the next? Also cover the use of server-side query logs to find the fields and datasets that agents misread.
